after_object.title: The Schur idempotent and the Schur functor for type-A q-Schur algebras
after_object.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n)\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the composition with $n$ parts equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above. 2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

u,\mu)|,&b	ext{ has distinct nonnegative entries and }|
u|=|\mu|,\0,&	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$ Here the tableau alphabet is the length of $\mu$; a shape with too many rows automatically has no such tableau ([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]). This function is alternating in the beta entries. It also obeys the branching identity $$d_\mu(b)=\sum_{\substack{C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}\|C|=z}}  d_{ ar\mu}(b-\mathbf1_C),$$ where $z$ is the last nonzero part of $\mu$ and $ ar\mu$ deletes that part. The selected entries are **decreased by one**, not replaced by $-1$. For a decreasing beta sequence this is the deletion of the largest semistandard entries: they occupy a horizontal strip, at most one box in each selected column. ## Statement

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the quantum characteristic ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and let $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for $n\ge0$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S^{\lambda}$ be the Hecke Specht module and $D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}$ its cell-form quotient ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is $e$-regular ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]); 2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\text{ is }e\text{-regular}\}$ is a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules; 3. $H$ is split semisimple if and only if $e>n$ (including $e=\infty$); when $e\le n$ the algebra has nonzero radical.

This is the exact root-of-unity replacement for the ordinary Specht classification. At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ it specialises to the classification of the simple $F[S_n]$-modules by $p$-regular partitions ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). No semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$, the algebra $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, its Hecke Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ and quotients $D^{\lambda}$ in the signed conjugate normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), and the numbers $e(F,q)$ and $[\ ]_q$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]).

[F1] ([[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]) The nonzero $D^{\lambda}$ form a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules; $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form on $S^{\lambda}$ is not identically zero.

[F2] ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) In the signed conjugate normalization $S^{\lambda}=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ and $D^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, where $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ is the Murphy cell module, $\theta$ is the involutive automorphism with $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$, and pullback along $\theta$ is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, nonzero modules and simplicity.

[F3] The complete relevant source proof is Mathas, Lemmas 3.35, 3.37, 3.38 and Theorem 3.39, printed pp. 32-34 (PDF pp. 38-40 of the guarded 79-page manuscript). The residue-character lower bound, ladder argument and **common factor of every Gram entry** are given explicitly below. The common factor is not a Gram determinant, and no full-hook product formula for all Specht determinants is asserted.

[F4] ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]) $\lambda$ is $e$-regular if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-restricted.

[F5] ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]) At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ the simple $F[S_n]$-modules are the heads of the Specht modules for the $p$-regular partitions.





## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Work first with Murphy cells $C^\eta=S_{\mathrm M}^\eta$ and their quotients $D_{\mathrm M}^\eta$. Their Jucys-Murphy action is triangular in the standard-tableau basis by [[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]. The cell-order multiplicity and diagonal-purity facts used here are [[cor-cellular-decomposition-matrices-are-dominance-unitriangular]]; the independent integral Murphy basis/straightening supplies the row-symmetrizer calculation via [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]. Thus restriction to the commutative algebra $\mathbb L$ generated by these elements has a one-dimensional-factor filtration, with the character of tableau $t$ given by the tuple $([\operatorname{res}_t(1)]_q,\ldots,[\operatorname{res}_t(n)]_q)$. Call a tableau of shape $\eta$ restricted if its tuple occurs in no standard tableau of a strictly smaller shape in the Murphy cell order. Cellularity gives $[C^\eta:D_{\mathrm M}^\rho]=0$ unless $\eta\unrhd\rho$ and gives diagonal multiplicity $1$ when the labelled quotient is nonzero. A restricted-tableau character therefore cannot be accounted for by any strictly smaller labelled simple. Every copy of such a character in $C^\eta|_{\mathbb L}$ must lie in its one diagonal copy of $D_{\mathrm M}^\eta|_{\mathbb L}$. Additivity of finite character multiplicities gives $$\dim D_{\mathrm M}^\eta\ge   |\operatorname{Std}_e(\eta)|.$$ This is the full residue-character argument of Mathas Lemma 3.35; it does not infer a nonzero labelled quotient merely from the existence of an unspecified composition factor. [F1, F3, given]

1.2 For the converse, carry out the row-symmetrizer calculation over the universal Laurent domain $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, then specialize $Q$ to $q$. For $\eta=(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_k)$ put $\delta^i=(\eta_i-\eta_{i+1},\ldots,\eta_k)$, of total size $\eta_i$. Let $g_i$ be the greatest common divisor of $[\gamma]!_Q$ over partitions $\gamma\vdash\eta_i$ dominating this row-difference composition, and put $g^\eta=\prod_i g_i$. The rowwise calculation shows that every cell-form entry is divisible by $g^\eta$. Here is the calculation, rather than a claim about the determinant. [given, F3]

2.1 If finite $e$ and $\eta$ is $e$-restricted, give the node $(a,b)$ ladder number $a+(e-1)b-e$. To construct the ladder tableau, place the last entry in a removable node of maximum ladder number, choosing the uppermost such node, and repeat on the remaining diagram. Removing this node leaves an $e$-restricted partition: increasing the preceding row difference to $e$ would put a node of greater ladder number in that preceding row, contradicting the choice; the other potentially changed difference cannot reach $e$ from a restricted partition. The chosen node is the lowest addable node with its residue compatible with the required dominance comparison. Induct on the number of entries: if a tableau of shape $\rho\unlhd\eta$ has the same residue tuple, the truncated shapes still have the required dominance comparison. The induction hypothesis forces the truncated tableau to equal the smaller ladder tableau. Its final node has the same residue; the extremal-node choice and dominance force that node to be the chosen one. Thus $\rho=\eta$ and the whole tableau is the ladder tableau. In particular this tableau is restricted. Step 1.1 then proves $D_{\mathrm M}^\eta\ne0$. This is Mathas Lemma 3.37 with its entire induction, completed on printed p. 33. [F3, step 1.1]

2.2 Write $x_\eta=x_{\eta_1}\cdots x_{\eta_k}$, the row symmetrizers on successive row intervals. For a row-standard tableau $t$, count the entries $1,\ldots,\eta_1$ in its rows; call their composition $\beta$. Sort these entries in reading order without changing the others, obtaining $u$ with $t=uw$, $w\in S_{\eta_1}$ and additive Coxeter length. The parabolic coset identity gives $$m_t x_{\eta_1}=Q^{\ell(w)}[\beta]!_Q\,m_u h$$ for some $h$ in the first-row parabolic algebra. The resulting permutation summand has row composition $(\eta_1,\eta_1-\beta_1,\ldots,\eta_k-\beta_k)$. If it is not dominated by $\eta$, its contribution is in the strictly higher Murphy ideal and vanishes in this cell. Otherwise the partial-sum inequalities give $\beta\unrhd\delta^1$, so $g_1$ divides $[\beta]!_Q$ (the reordered partition dominates $\beta$ and has the same factorial). Straighten while keeping the first row fixed: only tableaux agreeing with the canonical first row remain. Repeat the identical argument on the remaining rows. After row $i$ the common factor is $g_1\cdots g_i$ and all surviving tableaux agree with the first $i$ canonical rows. At $i=k$ only the canonical tableau remains. Hence $x_\eta T_{d(t)}x_\eta$ has coefficient divisible by $g^\eta$ on $x_\eta$ modulo higher shapes. The product definition of the cell form therefore makes every Gram entry divisible by $g^\eta$. This is Mathas Lemma 3.38, including its final row-induction step on printed p. 34. [F3, step 1.2]

2.3 For $e>n$, including $e=\infty$, no two distinct standard tableaux have the same residue tuple. Indeed, at the first unequal step their preceding diagram has size $m-1$; its distinct addable-corner contents have nonzero difference of absolute value at most $m\le n$. The identity $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ makes their residues distinct. Induction recovers the whole tableau and shape from the tuple. Thus all tableaux are restricted in the sense of step 1.1, giving $\dim D_{\mathrm M}^\eta\ge|\operatorname{Std}(\eta)|= \dim C^\eta$. As the quotient cannot have larger dimension, equality holds and every Murphy form has zero radical. This also proves the nonzero criterion at $e=\infty$, where every partition is restricted. [given, step 1.1]

3.1 If $\eta$ is not $e$-restricted, choose $i$ with $\eta_i-\eta_{i+1}\ge e$. Every partition $\gamma$ in the definition of $g_i$ has $\gamma_1\ge\eta_i-\eta_{i+1}\ge e$, so $[e]!_Q$ divides every $[\gamma]!_Q$ and hence divides their gcd $g_i$. It divides $g^\eta$. After specialization, $[e]!_q=0$ and every Gram entry vanishes by step 2.2. Thus the form is identically zero and $D_{\mathrm M}^\eta=0$. Together with step 2.1 this proves the finite-$e$ Murphy criterion. The empty partition at $n=0$ has the one-dimensional unit cell directly. [F3, step 2.1, step 2.2]

3.2 Derive split semisimplicity without the erroneous hook-determinant shortcut. Put $f_\eta=\dim C^\eta$ and $d_\eta=\dim D_{\mathrm M}^\eta$, with $d_\eta=0$ when that quotient is zero. The cellular basis gives $\dim H=\sum_\eta f_\eta^2$. On each nonzero quotient, the nondegenerate quotient form and the cell multiplication rule supply every rank-one operator, so $H\to\operatorname{End}_F(D_{\mathrm M}^\eta)$ is surjective. These kernels are distinct maximal two-sided ideals because the simple modules are pairwise nonisomorphic; the Chinese remainder theorem makes the product map surjective. Its kernel is the intersection of annihilators of all simple modules, namely $\operatorname{rad}H$ by the complete cellular classification. Hence $$\dim(H/\operatorname{rad}H)=\sum_\eta d_\eta^2.$$ When $e>n$, step 2.3 gives $d_\eta=f_\eta$ for every shape, so the kernel is zero and $H$ is a product of full matrix algebras over $F$. When finite $e\le n$, the **Murphy** row cell $(n)$ has form norm $\sum_{w\in S_n}q^{\ell(w)}=[n]!_q=0$, by $x_{(n)}^2=[n]!_q x_{(n)}$. Its quotient is zero but its dimension is $1$. Since $d_\eta\le f_\eta$ for every other shape, the displayed dimension sum is strictly smaller than $\dim H$, so $\operatorname{rad}H\ne0$. The ordinary row Specht is not used as a degenerate example: its normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy cell. This proves part 3. [F1, F2, step 2.3]

4.1 Translate the criterion by the actual signed-conjugate Definition: $D^\lambda=(D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda'})^\theta$. Exact involutive pullback preserves nonzero modules. Thus $D^\lambda\ne0$ precisely when $\lambda'$ is restricted, equivalently when $\lambda$ is regular. The nonzero Murphy quotients are absolutely simple and exhaust the simple modules; applying the same automorphism to all of them preserves these properties. This proves parts 1 and 2. At $q=1$ the actual all-field polytabloid/form bridge gives the group convention, and $e=p$ in positive characteristic. Part 1 then specializes exactly to the published $p$-regular classification. No statement that every zero-form Specht is reducible is made, and no choice principle is used. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 3.1, step 2.3] ∎

[F1] ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) $S^{\lambda}=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ and $D^{\mu}=(D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ for the conjugate partitions, where $S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}$ is the Murphy cell module and $\theta$ is the involutive automorphism $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$; pullback along $\theta$ is exact and preserves submodules, quotients, composition multiplicities and simplicity.

[F2] ([[cor-cellular-decomposition-matrices-are-dominance-unitriangular]]) For the Murphy cellular basis of $H$ the composition multiplicity $[S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]$ satisfies $[S^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ for nonzero $D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}$ and is zero unless $\nu\unrhd\rho$.

[F3] ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) Conjugation reverses dominance: $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ if and only if $\mu\unrhd\lambda$.

[F4] ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]) $D^{\mu}\ne0$ exactly for the $e$-regular $\mu$.

2.2 Diagonal: taking $\lambda=\mu$ in step 1.1 gives $d_{\mu\mu}=[S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 Assembly: steps 2.1 and 2.2 are exactly the two claims; ordering the rows and columns of $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ by any linear extension of dominance displays the unitriangular shape, and no off-diagonal entry is determined by the cellular structure. before_object.statement: Let $R$ be an integral domain, $q\in R^{\times}$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $S(d,n)$ be the q-Schur algebra with Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). For a partition $\lambda$ of $n$ with at most $d$ parts and a weight (composition of $n$ with at most $d$ parts) $\mu$, let $G^{\lambda}_{\mu}\in R$ be the determinant of the Gram matrix of the cell form of $W^{\lambda}$ restricted to its $\mu$-weight space, computed with respect to the semistandard basis. Let $\beta=\beta(\lambda)=(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n)$ be the beta sequence $\beta_i=\lambda'_i+n-i$ of $\lambda$ ([[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]], [[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) and let $h^{\lambda}_{ab}=\lambda_a-b+\lambda'_b-a+1$ be the hook length of the node $(a,b)\in[\lambda]$, with leg length $l^\lambda_{ab}$ ([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]). Then $$G^{\lambda}_{\mu}=q^{N}\prod_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\ b<c}}\left(\frac{[h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_q}{[h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_q}\right)^{d_{\mu}(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots,\beta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_n)},$$ where $N=N(\lambda,\mu)$ is the explicit integer $\sum_T\ell(d(\mathrm{last}(T)))$ summed over the semistandard $\lambda$-tableaux $T$ of type $\mu$ (the degree of the corresponding semistandard basis vector), $d_{\mu}$ is the signed semistandard multiplicity of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]] and $[\ \ ]_q$ are the quantum integers ([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]). The exponent has the exact combinatorial interpretation of Lemma 5.26: $$d_{\mu}(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ab},\dots,\beta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_n)=(-1)^{l^{\lambda}_{ab}+l^{\lambda}_{ac}}\,|T_0(\eta,\mu)|$$ whenever $\eta$ is obtained from $\lambda$ by unwrapping the removable border strip $R^{\lambda}_{ac}$ (the hook of $(a,c)$, of size $h^{\lambda}_{ac}$) and re-wrapping it with its lowest node in column $b$, and it is zero otherwise ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). The product is interpreted in $R$ after pairing all numerator and denominator factors, so the displayed formula represents an element of $R$ even though individual factors need not be units, and the theorem is stated over an integral domain, not only over a field.

## Statement

Let $R$ be an integral domain, $q\in R^\times$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module of $S(d,n)$ for a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts. For a composition $\mu$ of $n$ of length $d$, let $G^\lambda_\mu$ be the Gram determinant of its $\mu$-weight space in the semistandard basis ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Put $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+n-j$ and $h_{ab}=\lambda_a-b+\lambda'_b-a+1$. Then $$G^\lambda_\mu=q^N\prod_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\b<c}}  \left(\frac{[h_{ab}]_q}{[h_{ac}]_q}\right)^{  d_\mu(\beta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c)},$$ where $N=\sum_{T\in T_0(\lambda,\mu)}\ell(d(\operatorname{last}(T)))$. Here $\operatorname{last}(T)$ is the least-dominant standardization in the fiber of $T$, and $d_\mu$ is the exact alternating semistandard number of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. **Both beta shifts use the same removed hook length $h_{ac}$.**

The exponent is the sorting sign times $|T_0(\eta,\mu)|$ if that balanced beta sequence has distinct nonnegative entries and recovers $\eta$; it is zero otherwise. Equivalently, remove the rim strip $R_{ac}$ and rewrap its $h_{ac}$ boxes with lowest node in column $b$. The sign is the parity of the heights of the removed strip and the newly added strip, the latter measured in the new diagram $\eta$; it is not generally the sum of two old $\lambda$ hook legs ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

Form the product first in the universal field $\mathbb Q(Q)$. It equals a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, namely the universal integral Gram determinant divided by its displayed unit $Q^N$. Over $R$ the formula means the specialization of that Laurent polynomial. It does not require inverting a vanishing hook number or evaluating $0/0$. All weights and $d<n$ are retained; an empty weight space has determinant $1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The normalized semistandard maps, weight projections and Weyl cell form of the q-Schur Definition; the beta symbols and branching identity; and the hook-to-bead-gap correspondence in the cited suppliers.

[F1] The ordinary cell maps have the normalization $\varphi_{ST}(m_\nu h)=m_{ST}h$, with $m_{ST}=\sum_{\mu(s)=S,\nu(t)=T}m_{st}$. Their star swaps the indices, and their four-index cell product defines the Weyl form ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The actual regular corner identifies this product with the Murphy product with factor $1$ ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F2] Over $K=\mathbb Q(Q)$, the corrected intrinsic Murphy seminormal basis has its unitriangular normalization, adjacent-generator action and self-adjoint JM operators ([[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]]). For a semistandard $T$ and node $(i,j)$ of entry $v$, its predecessor set is precisely $$\Gamma_T(i,j)=\{(k,l):l<j,\ T(k,l)<v,\  T(k',l)>v\text{ for every }k'>k\}.$$ Equivalently $T(k,l)<v<T(k+1,l)$ with sentinel $+\infty$ below the column. Both inequalities are strict; an equal $v$ below excludes that column. Define $$\gamma_T:=\prod_{(i,j)}\prod_{(k,l)\in\Gamma_T(i,j)}  \frac{[j-i+k-l+1]_Q}{[j-i+k-l]_Q}.$$ The standard-tableau version is defined by the same rule.

[F3] The signed Kostka numbers satisfy $d_\mu(a)=\sum_{|C|=z}d_{\bar\mu}(a-\mathbf1_C)$, with zero values for repeated or negative beta entries ([[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Preserve small alphabets. Enlarge to $D=\max(d,n)$ temporarily. The sum of permutation summands with types supported on the first $d$ letters is a literal summand of the $D$-alphabet permutation module, with projection $p$ and $pS(D,n)p=S(d,n)$. The normalized maps whose two types have that support, their cell multiplication and their Weyl form coefficients are unchanged. Every semistandard shape with these types has at most $d$ rows. Thus proving the weight norm in the enlarged algebra, where the regular corner exists, proves the original norm as well. No hypothesis $d\ge n$ is added. [given, F1]

1.2 Compute the standard norms. For the canonical standard tableau, $\gamma_{t^\lambda}$ telescopes rowwise to $[\lambda]!_Q$, also its norm by $x_\lambda^2=[\lambda]!_Qx_\lambda$. If $s$ dominates $t=s(i,i+1)$, the adjacent action gives $f_t=f_s(T_i+\alpha)$ with $\alpha=1/[\rho]_Q$. Contravariance, orthogonality and the quadratic relation imply $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=(Q+\alpha)(1-\alpha) \langle f_s,f_s\rangle$. The two swapped predecessor ratios give $\gamma_t=Q^{-1}(Q+\alpha)(1-\alpha)\gamma_s$: use $[\rho+1]=1+Q[\rho]$ and $[\rho-1]=Q^{-1}([\rho]-1)$. Increasing-length adjacent swaps of incomparable boxes reach every standard tableau, so $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_t$. [F1, F2]

2.1 Compute the semistandard norms, including the missing scalar. Sums of JM elements over each label block commute with the corresponding row symmetrizer. Evaluation of the normalized map at $m_\mu$ gives their triangular action with leading eigenvalues $\sum_{T(i,j)=k}[j-i]_Q$. The joint eigenvalues distinguish $T$ over $K$: for every initial-label subshape they give its content multiset, whose diagonal counts determine the Young diagram. Finite triangular orthogonalization therefore gives $\psi_T=\varphi_T+$ more dominant terms. Let $U_T,V_T$ be the mutually adjoint cell maps between this weight and the regular weight, and let $\pi_t$ be the product of the axial ratios at standard predecessors with the **same** $T$-entry. Evaluation at $m_\mu$ gives $V_Tf_t=\pi_t\psi_T$: at the first standardization its scalar is the factorial of the row-intersection subgroup, also the telescoped $\pi_t$; an adjacent swap within a label block multiplies both scalars by $Q+\alpha$, since that row symmetrizer has $T_i$-eigenvalue $Q$. Finite bubble sorting connects the standardizations, proving the scalar for every $t$ in the fiber. For $t=\operatorname{last}(T)$, the strict boundary in [F2] partitions the standard predecessor set into $\Gamma_T$ and these same-entry predecessors, so $\gamma_t=\pi_t\gamma_T$. Also $U_T\psi_T$ has leading coefficient $1$ at $f_t$, all other terms more dominant, by the normalized map and the unitriangular basis changes. Hence adjointness gives $$\pi_t\langle\psi_T,\psi_T\rangle  =\langle f_t,U_T\psi_T\rangle  =Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_t,$$ so $\langle\psi_T,\psi_T\rangle=Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_T$. The transition determinant is $1$, yielding $G^\lambda_\mu=Q^N g^\lambda_\mu$ with $g^\lambda_\mu=\prod_T\gamma_T$. No norm is replaced by $Q^{\ell}$ alone. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 Prove the normalized beta product at the level of formal exponents. For $h\ge1$ put $$A_h(\beta,\mu)=-\sum_{b\ne c,\ \beta_b-h<\beta_c}  d_\mu(\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c).$$ A nonzero term requires $0\le\beta_b-h$, so the product is finite. Repeated beta entries cancel by exchanging the equal indices; a negative entry cannot become a valid term because, if it is the receiver, the lowered donor is still smaller. Thus these invalid sequences contribute zero exponents. Delete the largest semistandard label, occurring $z$ times in column feet $C$, to get $\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu$. The strict predecessor boundary excludes every column also in $C$. Consequently the literal exponent $E_h$ in $g$ obeys $$E_h(\beta,\mu)=\sum_{|C|=z}E_h(\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu)  +\sum_{|C|=z}\sum_{b\notin C,c\in C}  (\mathbf1_{\beta_b-\beta_c+1=h}-\mathbf1_{\beta_b-\beta_c=h})  d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_C).$$ The final sum is exactly the axial ratio contributed by each deleted largest-label box. [F2, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 Verify the same recurrence for $A_h$. Apply [F3] to its summands and compare with $\sum_C A_h(\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu)$. Set $\delta=\beta_b-\beta_c-h$. The original condition is $\delta<0$ and the deleted one $\delta-\mathbf1_C(b)+\mathbf1_C(c)<0$. They differ only when $b\in C,c\notin C,\delta=0$ or $b\notin C,c\in C,\delta=-1$. In the first case, exchanging the two shifted beta entries turns the contribution into $-d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_{C'})$ with $C'=C-b+c$, giving the negative term of step 3.1. In the second case, the exchanged entries give $+d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_C)$, giving its positive term. Every other case cancels. At degree $0$ both exponent families vanish: a nonzero shifted empty beta sequence would have to exchange two entries with $h=\beta_b-\beta_c$, excluded by the strict condition. Induction gives $E_h=A_h$ and therefore $$g^\lambda_\mu=  \prod_{h\ge1}\prod_{b\ne c,\ \beta_b-h<\beta_c}  [h]_Q^{-d_\mu(\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c)}.$$ This proves the regrouping without copying the inconsistent signs in the printed display. [F3, step 3.1]

5.1 Convert to hooks. A surviving lowered bead $\beta_b-h$ is a nonnegative gap, so the bead-gap correspondence makes $h=h_{ab}$ for a node $(a,b)$. The remaining condition $\beta_c>\beta_b-h_{ab}=n-1-\lambda_a+a$ is equivalent to $c\le\lambda_a$; the paired nodes therefore lie in the same row. For $b<c$ write $h=h_{ab}$ and $k=h_{ac}$. Since $h-k=\beta_b-\beta_c$, the two ordered displaced sequences $\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c$ and $\beta-k\mathbf e_c+k\mathbf e_b$ exchange their two changed entries. Their signed numbers are negatives of each other, and their factors are exactly $([h]_Q/[k]_Q)^{d_\mu(\beta+k\mathbf e_b-k\mathbf e_c)}$. This proves the stated balanced hook product. Removing and rewrapping the $k$-strip is precisely this bead transfer; sorting counts its crossings, which are the heights of the removed and **new** strips. Colliding or negative sequences vanish by definition. [given, F3, step 4.1]

6.1 Specialize integrally. The semistandard form matrix has entries in $\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, so its determinant and $Q^{-N}G^\lambda_\mu$ are Laurent polynomials. Steps 2.1-3.1 identify the rational products with these same polynomials in $\mathbb Q(Q)$. Base change of the free semistandard basis and its form now proves the identity over the given domain, including singular specializations and weights of dimension zero. No individual vanishing ratio is evaluated. All constructions are finite; no choice principle is used. [given, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

before_object.strategy: By the definition of $\varphi_{ST}$, multiplying by $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ kills all semistandard basis elements whose type is not $\omega$, and for type $\omega$ the surviving elements are exactly the $\varphi_t$ with $t$ a standard $\lambda$-tableau; this identifies the corner $W^{\lambda}e$ with the free module on the Murphy basis of the Hecke cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{M}}$, proving (1) for Weyl modules. To identify the simple image, compare the cellular forms rather than assuming exactness preserves heads. The corner idempotent $e=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ satisfies $e^*=e$. The semistandard product $\varphi_{T^{\lambda},s}\varphi_{t,T^{\lambda}}$, evaluated at $m_{\lambda}$, is the Murphy product $m_{t^{\lambda},s}m_{t,t^{\lambda}}$; higher Schur shapes evaluate to higher Murphy shapes. Its scalar coefficient therefore identifies the form on $W^{\lambda}e$ with the cell form on $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Associativity and $e^*=e$ make $W^{\lambda}e$ orthogonal to $W^{\lambda}(1-e)$, so $\mathrm{rad}(W^{\lambda})e=\mathrm{rad}(W^{\lambda}e)$. The Weyl form is nonzero because its canonical semistandard projection has Gram value $1$, and the repaired cellular classification identifies $L^{\lambda}=W^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}(W^{\lambda})$. Exactness now gives $F(L^{\lambda})\cong S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}(S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M})=D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$, including the zero-form case. This quotient is nonzero exactly for the restricted shapes by Theorem 3.39; only then is it the actual Specht-module head. This proves (2). Part (3) follows by applying the exact functor to a composition series of $W^{\lambda}$ and using (1)-(2) termwise, the multiplicities of the $D^{\nu}_{\mathrm{M}}$ with $\nu$ $e$-restricted being preserved. This is Mathas, Proposition 4.19 with the signed convention made explicit above: $F(W^{\lambda'})=S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^{\theta}$ and $F(L^{\lambda'})=D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^{\theta}$. Applying the same involutive exact pullback to both modules preserves all composition multiplicities. The untwisted printedp25 warning is not used. No choice is used.

## Statement

Let $k$ be a field, $q\in k^\times$, $d\ge n$, and let $\mathcal F(X)=Xe$ be the right-module Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]. For each $\lambda\in\Lambda^+(d,n)$ let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module with Schur cell form $B_\lambda$ and nonzero simple head $L^\lambda$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Write $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ and $D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ for the independent Murphy cell module and its cell-form quotient ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal F(W^\lambda)\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ as right $H$-modules, and this isomorphism identifies $B_\lambda|_{W^\lambda e}$ exactly with the Murphy cell form. 2. $\mathcal F(L^\lambda)\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, including the zero quotient; it is nonzero exactly when $\lambda$ is $e_q$-restricted. 3. For every $e_q$-restricted $\nu\vdash n$, $$[W^\lambda:L^\nu]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)].$$

In the page's ordinary Dipper–James normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]), these identities become $$\mathcal F(W^{\lambda'})\cong(S^\lambda)^\theta,\qquad \mathcal F(L^{\lambda'})\cong(D^\lambda)^\theta.$$ The latter module is nonzero exactly for $e_q$-regular $\lambda$ and is zero otherwise. For $e_q$-regular $\nu$, $$[W^{\lambda'}:L^{\nu'}]=[S^\lambda:D^\nu].$$ The accepted ordinary polytabloid comparison identifies $S^\lambda$ with the historical DJ module $P(\lambda)$ and identifies their form radicals through an explicit unit factor. Thus the dictionary concerns the actual ordinary modules, not merely a renamed cell module. A zero Hecke cell-form quotient is not asserted to be its actual module head. No semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed, and $n=0$ is included.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, stable range and modules in the Statement; all modules are right modules and multiplication in $S=\operatorname{End}_H(M)$ is ordinary composition $(fg)(x)=f(g(x))$.

[F1] The actual projection $e$ onto $M^\omega=H$, for $\omega=(1^n,0^{d-n})$, satisfies $e^2=e$ and $eSe\cong H$ by left multiplication $\rho(h)(a)=ha$. The functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]).

[F2] The legitimate semistandard cellular construction is supported from $M^{\operatorname{type}(T)}$ to $M^{\operatorname{type}(S)}$ and sends its generating $m_{\operatorname{type}(T)}h$ to $m_{ST}h$; its star swaps $S,T$ and its right-cell coefficients fix the first index modulo higher shapes. The Weyl cell basis is $(w_T)_T$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Only the actual summand projections are weight idempotents; no assertion that all diagonal cellular elements are idempotent is used.

[F3] The independent Murphy cellular datum uses $m_{st}=T_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda T_{d(t)}$, with its higher ideal $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, right cell basis $(c_t)_t$ and form $G_\lambda$ characterized by $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv G_\lambda(c_s,c_t)m_{ab}$ modulo that ideal ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F4] The nonzero cell-form quotients are pairwise distinct absolutely irreducible modules; when the form is not identically zero its radical is the unique maximal submodule. The Murphy quotient $D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)$ is nonzero precisely for $e_q$-restricted $\nu$ ([[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]], [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]], [[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).

[F5] The genuine ordinary bridge gives $P(\alpha)\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\alpha')^\theta$ and an explicit unit-scaled form identity, hence $D_{\mathrm{DJ}}(\alpha)\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\alpha')^\theta$ including zero quotients. This is the page's signed Specht normalization, and $\theta$ is an involutive algebra automorphism whose pullback is exact ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

The functor $X\mapsto Xe$ is exact: for a short exact sequence, a lift $x$ of an element $y\in X''e$ yields the lift $xe$, and an element in the kernel lies in $X'$ and is fixed by $e$, hence lies in $X'e$. The tensor description uses the $(S,eSe)$-bimodule $Se$, which is a direct summand as a left $S$-module. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The support in [F2] gives $e\varphi_{ST}e=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(S),\omega}\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}\varphi_{ST}$ and $w_Te=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}w_T$. Semistandard tableaux of type $\omega$ have each label once and are exactly standard tableaux. For standard $s,t$, their defining sum $m_{st}$ has one term, so $\varphi_{st}|_H(a)=m_{st}a$ and $\rho^{-1}(\varphi_{st})=m_{st}$. Thus the higher Schur ideal cuts out exactly $I^{\rhd\lambda}$ in the corner. 4.1 Since $e^*=e$, contravariance gives $B_\lambda(xe,y(1-e))=B_\lambda(x,y(1-e)e)=0$. The decomposition $W^\lambda=W^\lambda e\oplus W^\lambda(1-e)$ is therefore orthogonal. Replacing the Weyl label by $\lambda'$ in steps 2.1 and 5.1 gives the ordinary dictionary, including zero quotients. Conjugation makes $\lambda'$ restricted precisely when $\lambda$ is regular. At $n=0$, $e=1$ and each form has value $1$, so the same proof includes the empty partition. [F4, F5, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

before_object.title: Separated Hecke residues give seminormal idempotents and bases
before_object.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)$ and assume $e>n$ (with $e=\infty$ allowed); let $\lambda\vdash n$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, and let $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ be the Murphy cell module with Murphy basis $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).
1. (**Separation**) If $s,t$ are standard $\lambda$-tableaux with $[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ for all $1\le k\le n$ then $s=t$. More precisely, if the q-content values agree for all $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ for some $i$, then $s=t$ or $t=s(i\ i+1)$.
2. (**Idempotents**) For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ define, inside the commutative algebra $F[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, $$F_t:=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\ \prod_{\substack{s\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\\[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q}}\frac{L_k-[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q}{[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q-[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q}$$ and put $f_t:=m_tF_t\in S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. All denominators are nonzero by (1) and the $f_t$ are well-defined spectral projectors: $f_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,f_t$, and $f_t=m_t+\sum_{s\rhd t}a_sm_s$ for suitable $a_s\in F$.
3. (**Orthogonal seminormal basis**) $\{f_t:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is a basis of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ satisfying $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$ and $\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda=\delta_{st}\langle f_t,f_t\rangle_\lambda$; it is the **seminormal basis** of the Murphy cell module.
4. (**Generator action**) Let $s$ be a standard $\lambda$-tableau, $1\le i<n$ and $t:=s(i\ i+1)$, and put $\rho:=\operatorname{content}_s(i)-\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)\in\mathbb Z$ (an integer; it equals $\operatorname{res}_s(i)-\operatorname{res}_t(i)$ in the source's notation). If $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $s$ then $f_sT_i=q\,f_s$; if they lie in the same column then $f_sT_i=-f_s$; otherwise $t$ is standard and $$f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)\,f_t-\frac{1}{[\rho]_q}f_s,\qquad \alpha_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&s\rhd t,\\[1mm]\dfrac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q},&t\rhd s,\end{cases}$$ where $[-\rho]_q$ is the extended quantum integer of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] and for the swapped tableau $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$. No semisimplicity of $H$ is assumed and no choice principle is used.
before_object.strategy: (1) is Lemma 3.32: when $e>n$ the nodes of equal $e$-residue lie on diagonal lines, so distinct removable nodes have distinct residues, and peeling off $n,n-1,\dots,1$ determines $t$ from its q-content sequence. (2),(3) are Proposition 3.33 and Theorem 3.34: the triangularity of [[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]] makes $F_t$ a projector annihilating strictly dominating tableaux; comparing $f_sL_k$ directly and using the associativity of the cellular form ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) gives $f_sF_t=\delta_{st}f_t$ and orthogonality. (4) is the coefficient computation of Theorem 3.34(ii): $f_sT_i$ is an eigenvector of every $L_k$ with $k\ne i,i+1$, so by (1) it lies in $\mathrm{span}(f_s,f_t)$; writing $f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)f_t+c_sf_s$ and multiplying on the right by $L_i$ recovers $c_s=-1/[\rho]_q$ from the relation $T_iL_i=T_iL_{i+1}-1-(q-1)L_{i+1}$ of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]], and the quadratic relation $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$ gives the product $\alpha_i(s)\alpha_i(t)=[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q/([\rho]_q[-\rho]_q)$ for the swapped tableau $t$; since $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$, the two standard cases have $\rho>0$ with $s\rhd t$ (branch $1$) and $\rho<0$ with $t\rhd s$ (branch $[1+\rho][1-\rho]/([\rho][-\rho])$). The stated branch assignment is the Mathas-Murphy seminormal coefficient system of Hu-Mathas (Example 3.11 with the axial distance (3.8), Lemma 3.12 and Proposition 3.17), which we verified directly in $H(S_3)$ ($\rho=2$, $q=3,5,7$) and $H(S_4)$ ($\rho=3$, $q=2$); the display of Theorem 3.34(ii) in the 1998 prepublication manuscript is inconsistent with the Hecke relations in the $t\rhd s$ case (exact computation in the batch notes), so the item uses the corrected form. The abstract cellular-algebra form of the same spectral construction is checked independently in Mathas-Soriano (separation condition, Proposition 4.13 and the appendix). No choice is used.

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)$ and assume $e>n$ (with $e=\infty$ allowed); let $\lambda\vdash n$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, and let $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ be the Murphy cell module with Murphy basis $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

(**Idempotents**) Let $\mathcal R_k$ be the set of distinct q-content values of the entry $k$ over standard tableaux of **all** partitions of $n$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ define $$F_t:=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\ \prod_{\substack{c\in\mathcal R_k\\        c\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q}}        \frac{L_k-c}{[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q-c}\in F[L_1,\ldots,L_n].$$ These are orthogonal idempotents of $H$; their actions on $S_{\mathrm M}^\lambda$ project onto the corresponding simultaneous eigenlines. (**Generator action**) Let $s$ be a standard $\lambda$-tableau, $1\le i<n$ and $t:=s(i\ i+1)$, and put $\rho:=\operatorname{content}_s(i)-\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)\in\mathbb Z$. If $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $s$ then $f_sT_i=q\,f_s$; if they lie in the same column then $f_sT_i=-f_s$; otherwise $t$ is standard and $$f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)\,f_t-\frac{1}{[\rho]_q}f_s,\qquad \alpha_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&s\rhd t,\\[1mm]\dfrac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q},&t\rhd s,\end{cases}$$ where $[-\rho]_q$ is the extended quantum integer of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] and for the swapped tableau $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$. No semisimplicity of $H$ is assumed and no choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e>n$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ and cell form ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), and the q-content values of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]].

[F1] ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]) $m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_vm_v$ in $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$; the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in them is central.

[F2] ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) For $e>n$ no $m$ with $1\le m\le n$ has $[m]_q=0$; more precisely, if two integer contents $c,c'$ with $|c-c'|\le n$ satisfy $[c]_q=[c']_q$ then $c=c'$.

[F3] ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) The cell form on $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is symmetric and associative, and the star anti-involution fixes each $L_k$; the Murphy basis is triangular along the dominance order on tableaux.

[F4] Source results: separation of q-content sequences for $e>n$ and the seminormal spectral construction are Mathas, Lemma 3.32, Proposition 3.33 and Theorem 3.34 (printed pp. 30-34); the coefficient system of part 4 as displayed is that of Hu-Mathas, Example 3.11 with the axial distance (3.8), Lemma 3.12 and Proposition 3.17, the 1998 manuscript's $t\rhd s$ branch being inconsistent with the Hecke relations. The abstract form of the spectral construction under the separation condition is Mathas, Proposition 4.13 with the appendix.





## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Reconstruct a tableau from its residue tuple. At a prefix of size $k-1$, two different addable corners have integer content difference of absolute value at most $k$. Since $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ and $e>n$, their q-contents differ. Starting with the empty diagram, the tuple thus recovers each added node and the final shape. For two tableaux of a fixed shape with identical entries' residues outside $i,i+1$, first reconstruct the common prefix through $i-1$, and reconstruct the common suffix by successively deleting the unique appropriate removable corner from the fixed final shape. The intervening skew diagram has two boxes; its only possible orders are the original order and its swap. This proves both separation assertions. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Diagonalize the commuting JM operators on a cell. Their triangular basis gives a filtration with one-dimensional joint characters indexed by standard tableaux. Those characters are distinct by step 1.1. For commuting triangular operators, the simultaneous generalized eigenspaces split along their distinct joint characters: the corresponding maximal ideals of the polynomial algebra are pairwise comaximal. Each joint character occurs once in this cell, so each generalized eigenspace is one-dimensional and hence an actual joint eigenline. This finite Chinese-remainder argument works over any field and needs no choice of a generic scalar or algebraic closure. The Lagrange product of the Statement is $1$ on its target tuple and $0$ on every other tuple. Applied to $m_t$, its triangular diagonal coefficient is $1$, and the other possible terms are strictly more dominant. Thus it gives the asserted $f_t$. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 Compute the diagonal coefficient using the **correctly ordered** JM relation $$T_iL_i=L_{i+1}T_i-(q-1)L_{i+1}-1.$$ For $k\ne i,i+1$, $T_i$ commutes with $L_k$. Consequently separation restricts $f_sT_i$ to the span of $f_s$ and $f_t$ if the swap is standard, or to $f_s$ alone otherwise. Write its coefficient of $f_s$ as $c_s$. The displayed relation gives $$c_s\bigl([\operatorname{content}_s(i)]_q-              [\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)]_q\bigr)    =-(q-1)[\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)]_q-1.$$ Its denominator is $q^{\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)}[\rho]_q$, while the numerator is $-q^{\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)}$, so $c_s=-1/[\rho]_q$. This does not claim that $T_i$ commutes with $L_i$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Verify the global algebra idempotents. By the independently proved classification and semisimplicity criterion, $e>n$ implies that all Murphy cells are simple and their direct sum is a faithful $H$-module ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]). On this faithful sum, the global products of the Statement act as the orthogonal joint-eigenline projectors just computed, and different shapes have disjoint tuples by step 1.1. Therefore their products satisfy $F_sF_t=\delta_{st}F_t$ in $H$ itself. A product using only same-shape contents would in general prove only its induced cell-module projection, not this global identity. [step 2.1]

3.2 The transition from $m_t$ to $f_t$ is unitriangular, so these vectors form a basis. For $s\ne t$, choose $k$ at which their q-contents differ. Self-adjointness $L_k^*=L_k$ and associativity give $$([\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q-    [\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q)\langle f_s,f_t\rangle=0.$$ The scalar is nonzero, proving orthogonality. The Lagrange action also gives $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.3 If the swap is not standard, the consecutive entries lie adjacently in one row or one column. Then $\rho=-1$ or $\rho=1$, respectively, and step 2.2 gives $c_s=q$ or $c_s=-1$. These are the stated row and column cases; the row action is $q$, not the scalar $1$ at a general parameter. [step 2.2]

4.1 Suppose the swap is standard. In the branch $s\rhd t$, the length-additive Murphy action has leading term $m_sT_i=m_t$; the unitriangular eigenbasis change then gives the off-diagonal coefficient $\alpha_i(s)=1$. Higher-dominance terms cannot alter the coefficient at $t$ in this two-dimensional eigenline span. This is the leading-term argument in the full proof of Mathas Theorem 3.34. In both branches the quadratic relation gives $$\alpha_i(s)\alpha_i(t)=q+(q-1)c_s-c_s^2  =\frac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q}.$$ The last equality follows directly from $[-\rho]_q=-q^{-\rho}[\rho]_q$ and the quantum-integer addition identities. Thus the opposite branch has exactly the displayed coefficient. This proves the generator formula without accepting the inconsistent branch in the 1998 manuscript. [step 3.2, step 2.2]

5.1 Steps 1.1-4.1 give all four claims. Split semisimplicity was derived from $e>n$ in step 3.1, not imposed as an additional hypothesis. The calculation concerns the intrinsic Murphy cell, and does not replace its ordinary-module comparison by an untwisted conjugate identification. All products and basis changes are finite; no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1] ∎

before_object.statement:

## Statement

Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, $\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$ the residue field, and let $\hat q\in R^{\times}$ satisfy $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$ in $R$; put $q:=\hat q+\pi R\in F^{\times}$. Let $d\ge1$, let $\lambda$ be a partition of $n$ with at most $d$ parts, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl module of the q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)=S(d,n)\otimes_RF$ with its Jantzen filtration $W^{\lambda}_F(i)$ with respect to $(R,\pi)$ ([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

1. (**Jantzen sum formula**) In the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $S_F(d,n)$-modules, $$\sum_{i>0}\bigl[W^{\lambda}_F(i)\bigr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\ b<c}}\Bigl(\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q}\bigr)-\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q}\bigr)\Bigr)\Bigl[W_F^{(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_n)}\Bigr],$$ where $\beta=\beta(\lambda)$ is the beta sequence of $\lambda$, $h^{\lambda}_{ab}$ are its hook lengths and the symbols are the virtual Weyl symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. 2. (**q-Schaper, $d\ge n$**) If $d\ge n$ and $\Pi$ denotes the Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], then applying $\Pi$ to (1) gives the corresponding identity for the Hecke Specht modules in the source's normalisation, that is, for the Murphy cell modules $\Pi(W^{\lambda}_F)=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ of [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]] (the Dipper-James form is obtained by conjugating partitions and applying the same $\theta$ pullback to every Hecke module), $$\sum_{i>0}\bigl[S^{\lambda}_F(i)\bigr]=\sum_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\ b<c}}\Bigl(\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q}\bigr)-\nu_\pi\bigl([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q}\bigr)\Bigr)\Bigl[S_F^{(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_b+h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_c-h^{\lambda}_{ac},\dots,\beta_n)}\Bigr]$$ in the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional $H_{F,q}(S_n)$-modules, with the virtual Specht symbols of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. The formula is a positive filtration-sum identity expressed in a signed Weyl/Specht basis. A single nonzero signed Weyl coefficient does not force the corresponding labelled simple factor: the entire right side must first be expanded and cancelled in simple classes. For a Weyl module and an off-head label $\nu$, the resulting multiplicity of $L^\nu$ is an upper bound for $[W^\lambda:L^\nu]$, and is positive exactly when that factor occurs in the radical. This does not give a general closed algorithm for decomposition numbers.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A PID $R$ with prime $\pi$, residue field $F$, $\hat q\in R^{\times}$ with $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$, the q-Schur algebra $S_F(d,n)$ and its Weyl modules with Jantzen filtrations ([[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]), and the virtual Weyl and Specht symbols ([[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]).

[F1] ([[thm-q-schur-weyl-weight-space-gram-determinant-hook-product]]) The Gram determinant of $W^{\lambda}$ on its $\nu$-weight space equals $q^{N}$ times the hook-ratio product $\prod_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],b<c}([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q}/[h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})^{d_{\mu}(\dots)}$; under $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$ every factor is nonzero in the domain $R$.

[F2] ([[lem-jantzen-layer-dimensions-equal-the-gram-determinant-valuation]]) The total dimension of the positive Jantzen layers on a non-degenerate form equals the $\pi$-adic valuation of its Gram determinant.

[F3] ([[lem-semistandard-weight-dimensions-detect-virtual-weyl-classes]]) Equality of all semistandard weight-space dimensions forces equality in the Grothendieck group of $S_F(d,n)$-modules.

[F4] The balanced displacement removes the $h_{ac}$-strip and adds the same number of boxes, preserving degree; its sign is the beta sorting sign ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

[F5] The exact Schur functor has integral corner isomorphism and exact restricted form factor $1$, with $e^*=e$ ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]). Filtration transport is proved below, rather than assumed from exactness.

[F6] Source results (Mathas, Theorem 5.31 and Corollary 5.32, printed pp. 58-60): the Jantzen sum formula for the q-Schur algebra and its transport to the Hecke side, with the coefficient $\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})$ and the virtual symbols.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Work on a fixed weight space of the lifted free Weyl module. Every hook quantum integer is nonzero because its index is at most $n$ and $[n]!_{\hat q}\ne0$ in the domain. The balanced Gram formula [F1] gives its determinant, and the unit power of $\hat q$ has valuation zero. The Jantzen Gram-valuation lemma [F2] thus gives the sum of positive filtration-submodule dimensions as $$\sum_{(a,b),(a,c),\ b<c}  (\nu_\pi([h_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h_{ac}]_{\hat q}))  d_\mu(\beta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c).$$ The signed number is exactly the weight dimension of the corresponding balanced virtual Weyl symbol, including zero and cutoff cases. [given, F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Apply step 1.1 to every weight. The Weyl weight-character matrix is unitriangular, so [F3] detects equality of Grothendieck classes and proves part 1. These are classes of the filtration submodules $W_F^\lambda(i)$, not their successive quotients and not simply the radical class. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Establish filtration transport before applying the exact functor. On the lifted Weyl module $W$, the identity $e^*=e$ makes $We\perp W(1-e)$. For $x\in We$ and every $i\ge0$, pairing $x$ with all of $W$ is divisible by $\pi^i$ exactly when its pairing with $We$ is. Thus $W(i)e=(We)(i)$. Reducing modulo $\pi$ commutes with the direct summand projection, giving $W_F(i)e=(We)_F(i)$. The actual corner isomorphism and factor-$1$ form identity [F5] identify the latter with the Murphy Specht filtration. Applying the exact functor to the proved Weyl-class identity therefore transports each submodule and every signed term, proving part 2 even when a reduced cell form is identically zero. For the ordinary convention, apply the same $\theta$ to both modules and conjugate the labels; the independently proved Laurent-unit form factor preserves these divisibility filtrations as well. [F5, step 2.1]

4.1 Explain the valid multiplicity information. The Weyl form has nonzero simple head, $W_F(1)=\operatorname{rad}W_F$, and $W_F(i)\subseteq\operatorname{rad}W_F$ for $i>0$. Consequently for $\nu\ne\lambda$ its actual multiplicity in $W_F$ is its radical multiplicity, bounded above by its multiplicity in the whole positive sum. This whole-sum multiplicity is positive if and only if that factor occurs in the radical, since the first submodule is the radical and later ones lie inside it. No such conclusion is drawn from an individual positive or negative Weyl coefficient before cancellation. All claims follow from steps 1.1-3.1 and this submodule inclusion. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

The two preceding constraints on the decomposition matrix of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ are real but limited, and neither solves the general problem.

(i) Dominance unitriangularity ([[cor-type-a-hecke-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]]) determines only the diagonal entries $d_{\mu\mu}=1$ and the vanishing region $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\Rightarrow\mu\unrhd\lambda$; it gives no value for an off-diagonal entry.

(ii) The q-Schaper/Jantzen sum formula ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]]) is an identity for the sum of the positive Jantzen filtration submodules. Its individual signed hook terms are not multiplicity bounds. After the whole virtual sum is expanded in simple classes and all cancellations are performed, its nonnegative simple coefficients bound the corresponding radical composition multiplicities from above; it neither determines a general multiplicity nor produces a positive combinatorial rule.

Special coefficient regimes and low-rank calculations determine additional entries (canonically based, weight-one, and small-$n$ cases), but the classification of irreducible Specht modules in arbitrary positive characteristic is a known open problem, and no general closed formula for the decomposition numbers of $S_n$ in a fixed positive characteristic is claimed anywhere on this page. This remark records the boundary; it carries no proof obligation and no choice principle.

## Remarks

The two cited results are the constraints proved on this page: unitriangularity is a vanishing statement about the dominance order, and the q-Schaper formula expresses the sum of the positive Jantzen filtration submodules as a virtual combination of Weyl symbols whose coefficients are $\pi$-adic valuations of hook q-integers. Neither statement computes an individual off-diagonal decomposition number in general, and the remark is not used as a supplier to prove any replacement claim.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. In $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]) for $n\ge4$ are $$L_1=0,\quad L_2=q^{-1}T_{(1,2)},\quad L_3=q^{-1}T_{(2,3)}+q^{-2}T_{(1,3)},\quad L_4=q^{-1}T_{(3,4)}+q^{-2}T_{(2,4)}+q^{-3}T_{(1,4)},$$ and in general $L_k=\sum_{j<k}q^{j-k}T_{(j,k)}$. For the standard tableau $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3&4\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ of shape $(3,1)$ the contents of the entries $k=1,2,3,4$ are $0,-1,1,2$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]), so the diagonal eigenvalues of $L_1,\dots,L_4$ on the Murphy vector $m_t$ are $[0]_q=0$, $[-1]_q=-q^{-1}$, $[1]_q=1$ and $[2]_q=1+q$; the triangular correction terms $\sum_{v\rhd t}a_vm_v$ are present in general ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]) in the Murphy basis, even in the semisimple range. In the separated range, replacing $m_t$ by the seminormal vector $f_t$ removes these correction terms, as proved in [[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]]. At $q=1$ the four elements specialize to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy elements $X_1=0$, $X_2=(1\,2)$, $X_3=(1\,3)+(2\,3)$, $X_4=(1\,4)+(2\,4)+(3\,4)$ and the eigenvalues to $0,-1,1,2$, the standard contents of $t$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, $q\in R^{\times}$, the Hecke algebra $H_{R,q}(S_n)$, the Jucys-Murphy elements and q-contents ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]), the content vector of a standard tableau ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]), and the q=1 specialization $H_{R,1}(S_n)\cong R[S_n]$ ([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

[F1] ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]) $L_k=\sum_{j<k}q^{j-k}T_{(j,k)}$; $[m]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1}$ for $m\ge0$, $[-m]_q=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, and $[m]_1=m$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$.

before_object.title: Residue sequences need not separate when e is at most n
before_object.statement: The hypothesis $e>n$ in [[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]] cannot be dropped. Take $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$ (so $e=e(\mathbb C,-1)=2$, [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), $n=3$ and $\lambda=(2,1)$. The two distinct standard tableaux $s=\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$ and $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ have contents $\operatorname{content}_s(1),\operatorname{content}_s(2),\operatorname{content}_s(3)=0,1,-1$ and $\operatorname{content}_t(1),\operatorname{content}_t(2),\operatorname{content}_t(3)=0,-1,1$, and since $[m]_{-1}=[m]+(-1)^{m-1}[1]_{-1}$ reduces modulo $e=2$ one has $[1]_{-1}=1=[-1]_{-1}$ ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] for the extended quantum integers). Hence $$([\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}=(0,1,1)=([\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}\quad(q=-1):$$ the q-content sequences collide although $s\ne t$, so the separation conclusion of the theorem fails. Moreover the interpolation denominator for $k=2$ is the difference $[\operatorname{content}_t(2)]_q-[\operatorname{content}_s(2)]_q=[-1]_{-1}-[1]_{-1}=0$, so the projector $F_t$ of the theorem is not defined in this case; the same collision $\rho\equiv0\bmod e$ makes $[\rho]_q=0$ in the generator formula of the theorem's part 4. Consequently no seminormal basis is available beyond the semisimple range, and the theorem's hypothesis $e>n$ is optimal.
before_object.strategy: Compute the contents from the definitions and compare the quantum integers at $q=-1$; the collision occurs exactly because the two contents differ by $e=2$. This is the boundary of Mathas's Lemma 3.32, whose proof uses $e>n$ so that equal-residue nodes lie on diagonal lines, and it is the counterexample to the naive extension of Theorem 3.34 beyond its hypothesis. No choice is used.

## Statement refuted

The hypothesis $e>n$ in [[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]] cannot be dropped. Take $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$ (so $e=e(\mathbb C,-1)=2$, [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), $n=3$ and $\lambda=(2,1)$. The two distinct standard tableaux $s=\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$ and $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ have contents $\operatorname{content}_s(1),\operatorname{content}_s(2),\operatorname{content}_s(3)=0,1,-1$ and $\operatorname{content}_t(1),\operatorname{content}_t(2),\operatorname{content}_t(3)=0,-1,1$, and the extended quantum-integer identity gives $[1]_{-1}=1=[-1]_{-1}$, since $[-1]_{-1}=-(-1)^{-1}[1]_{-1}=1$. Hence $$([\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}=(0,1,1)=([\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}\quad(q=-1):$$ the q-content sequences collide although $s\ne t$, so the separation conclusion of the theorem fails. The difference of the two putative separating eigenvalues at $k=2$ is $[-1]_{-1}-[1]_{-1}=0$. Thus interpolation cannot distinguish the two tableaux: a formula that excludes equal values may still define a polynomial, but it is not a separating projector for these two labels. The attempted generator formula has axial distance $\rho=2$ and $[\rho]_{-1}=0$. In fact $L_2$ has a nontrivial Jordan block on this cell, so this cell has no simultaneous JM-eigenbasis. This explicit example shows that the uniform separation hypothesis $e>n$ cannot be dropped; it does not claim that every individual cell at every parameter with $e\le n$ lacks a seminormal basis.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field $\mathbb C$, $q=-1\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, $n=3$, the standard tableaux $s,t$ of shape $(2,1)$ above, and the q-integers of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]].

[F1] ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) $e(\mathbb C,-1)=2$: the least $m\ge1$ with $[m]_{-1}=0$ is $m=2$, since $[2]_{-1}=1+q=0$ and $[1]_{-1}=1\ne0$.

[F2] ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]) The q-content value of an entry is $[\operatorname{content}]_q$ with $[m]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1}$ for $m\ge0$ and $[-m]_q=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$; at $q=-1$ one has $[1]_{-1}=1$ and $[-1]_{-1}=-(-1)^{-1}[1]_{-1}=1$.

[F3] ([[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]]) Under the hypothesis $e>n$ the q-content sequence determines the standard tableau, and the denominators of the spectral projectors are nonzero.




## Counterexample

1.1 Contents of the two tableaux: for $s$ with rows $(1,2)$ and $(3)$ the nodes are $(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)$ for $1,2,3$, giving contents $0,1,-1$; for $t$ with rows $(1,3)$ and $(2)$ the nodes are $(1,1),(2,1),(1,2)$ for $1,2,3$, giving contents $0,-1,1$. [given]

2.1 Collision: by [F1] and [F2], $[2]_{-1}=0$ and $[1]_{-1}=[-1]_{-1}=1$; hence $[\operatorname{content}_s(1)]_{q}=0=[\operatorname{content}_t(1)]_q$, $[\operatorname{content}_s(2)]_q=1=[\operatorname{content}_t(2)]_q$ and $[\operatorname{content}_s(3)]_q=1=[\operatorname{content}_t(3)]_q$, so the two q-content sequences coincide even though $s\ne t$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 Interpolation and axial distance. The eigenvalue difference that would be needed to distinguish $s$ and $t$ at $k=2$ is $1-1=0$. Equal-value exclusion in a polynomial product does not make its literal denominators zero; it instead loses the factor that could distinguish these tuples. No polynomial in the JM operators can provide the two distinct joint-eigenvalue labels used in the separated-range construction. For the swap of $2$ and $3$, $\rho=1-(-1)=2$ and $[2]_{-1}=0$, so the displayed separated-range generator formula is undefined here. [step 2.1, F1, F3]

4.1 Verify the failure of a JM-eigenbasis on this cell directly. Put $m_s=1+T_1$ and $m_t=(1+T_1)T_2$ modulo the higher row-shape ideal. The quadratic relation gives $m_sT_1=q m_s$. The higher row symmetrizer is $1+T_1+T_2+T_1T_2+T_2T_1+T_1T_2T_1$, so its vanishing in this cell gives $m_tT_1=-m_s-m_t$. At $q=-1$, since $L_2=q^{-1}T_1=-T_1$, it follows that $m_sL_2=m_s$ and $m_tL_2=m_s+m_t$. Thus $L_2-I$ is nonzero and $(L_2-I)^2=0$ on this two-dimensional cell. It is not diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$, so a simultaneous JM-eigenbasis cannot exist on this cell. Together with step 2.1 this supplies the claimed concrete boundary counterexample, without making a universal claim about all cells outside the separated range. [given, F2, step 3.1] ∎

## Example

Take $R=\mathbb C[\hat q]_{(1+\hat q)}$, the prime element $\pi=1+\hat q$ (so that $F=\mathbb C$ and $q:=\hat q+\pi R$ specialises to $-1$, giving $e=2$), and $\lambda=(3,2)$, $n=5$. Evaluating the q-Schaper virtual sums ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula, thm-q-schur-weyl-weight-space-gram-determinant-hook-product, thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules, thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]) with the hook valuations $\nu_\pi([2]_{\hat q})=\nu_\pi([4]_{\hat q})=1$, $\nu_\pi([3]_{\hat q})=\nu_\pi([1]_{\hat q})=0$ gives, in the source's normalisation, $$\sum_{i>0}\bigl[W^{(3,2)}_F(i)\bigr]=\bigl[W^{(3,1^2)}_F\bigr]+\bigl[W^{(2^2,1)}_F\bigr]-\bigl[W^{(1^5)}_F\bigr],\qquad \sum_{i>0}\bigl[S^{(3,2)}_F(i)\bigr]=2\bigl[D^{(2^2,1)}_{\mathrm{M}}\bigr].$$ Further Jantzen calculations give $W^{(1^5)}_F=L^{(1^5)}_F$, $W^{(2^2,1)}_F=L^{(2^2,1)}_F$ and $W^{(3,1^2)}_F\sim L^{(3,1^2)}_F+L^{(2^2,1)}_F+L^{(1^5)}_F$, so at the level of the sum formula alone one gets $d_{(3,2),(3,1^2)}=1$ and only the bound $d_{(3,2),(2^2,1)}\in\{1,2\}$. The computed entry is consistent with the dominance bound $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\Rightarrow\mu\unrhd\lambda$ of [[cor-type-a-hecke-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The DVR $R=\mathbb C[\hat q]_{(1+\hat q)}$, unit $\hat q$, uniformizer $\pi=1+\hat q$, residue field $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$, $e=2$, and $d\ge5$. All displayed Weyl modules are for this $S_F(d,5)$.

[F1] The corrected **balanced** sum formula and its signs are [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] and [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. The weight Gram product is [[thm-q-schur-weyl-weight-space-gram-determinant-hook-product]].

[F2] $v([h]_{\hat q})$ is $1$ for $h=2,4$ and $0$ for $h=1,3,5$; the even roots are simple over $\mathbb C$. The Weyl forms have nonzero simple heads and their first reduced Jantzen submodule is the radical.

[F3] The Schur functor has factor-$1$ form restriction and preserves the multiplicities of restricted simple factors ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]). The restricted labels among the shapes below are $(2,2,1)$, $(2,1^3)$ and $(1^5)$; $(3,2)$ and $(3,1^2)$ have zero Murphy form quotients ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

The identities $[2]=1+\hat q$, $[4]=(1+\hat q)(1+\hat q^2)$ and evaluation of the odd quantum integers at $-1$ prove [F2]. These values refer to this lift, not an arbitrary field or lift with quantum characteristic $2$. [given, F1, F2]

The pair $(1,1),(1,2)$ gives $(9,2,3,1,0)$, which sorts to the beta sequence of $(1^5)$ with sign $-1$ and coefficient $v(4)-v(3)=1$. The pair $(1,1),(1,3)$ gives $(7,5,2,1,0)$, shape $(2,2,1)$ with sign $+1$ and coefficient $v(4)-v(1)=1$. The pair $(2,1),(2,2)$ gives $(7,4,3,1,0)$, shape $(3,1^2)$ with sign $+1$ and coefficient $v(2)-v(1)=1$. The remaining pair has repeated beta entries and vanishes. Thus the first displayed Weyl identity follows by direct substitution. [F1, F2]

2.1 Compute the smaller rows rather than assuming them. The same calculation for $(3,1^2)$ gives $\sum_{i>0}[W^{(3,1^2)}(i)]=[W^{(2,2,1)}]+[W^{(1^5)}]$: the pairs with hook lengths $(5,2)$ and $(2,1)$ give those two terms, while the $(5,1)$ coefficient is zero. For $(2,2,1)$, the only nonzero symbols arise from pairs $(4,2)$ and $(3,1)$, both of valuation difference zero. For $(2,1^3)$ the sole pair is $(5,1)$, also zero; $(1^5)$ has no pair. Hence these three Weyl modules have zero positive sums and zero radicals, so they equal their simple heads. For $(3,1^2)$ each displayed simple occurs once in the positive sum; because its first submodule is the radical and later ones lie inside it, both radical multiplicities are exactly $1$. 3.1 Supply the actual dimension argument. The regular-weight Gram product for the Murphy cell $(2,2,1)$ is $$\hat q^7\frac{[4]_{\hat q}}{[2]_{\hat q}}[3]_{\hat q}^4   =\hat q^7(1+\hat q^2)[3]_{\hat q}^4,$$ since its two signed symbols have shapes $(1^5)$ and $(2,1^3)$ with standard-tableau counts $1$ and $4$. The form of $(3,2)$ is identically zero by its nonrestricted label, so its first submodule is the whole five-dimensional cell. 4.1 A further consistency check is the regular-weight Gram product $\hat q^8[3]_{\hat q}[4]_{\hat q}^4[2]_{\hat q}^6$ for $(3,2)$, whose valuation is $10$, agreeing with two five-dimensional positive Specht submodules. This is a check of the complete balanced formula; it is not the unsupported full-hook product used in the former classification proof. [F1, step 1.2, step 3.1]

5.1 Translate simultaneously by $\theta$ and conjugation. The actual ordinary/Murphy module-and-form comparison sends the isomorphism of step 3.1 to $S_{\mathrm{DJ}}^{(2,2,1)}\cong D_{\mathrm{DJ}}^{(3,2)}$. The partition $(2,2,1)$ is not regular, so its own **cell-form quotient** is zero; this does not say its actual head is zero, since the module itself is simple. The dominance inequality $(3,2)\unrhd(2,2,1)$ agrees with the ordinary-convention unitriangular bound. This proves every claimed numeric conclusion. [F3, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement refuted

A cellular algebra need not be semisimple, its cell modules need not be simple, and a labelled cell-form quotient $D^{\lambda}$ may vanish although the cell module $C^{\lambda}$ is nonzero.

(a) Abstract degenerate instance: let $F$ be a field and $A=F[x]/(x^2)$, with $\Lambda=\{2\rhd1\}$ ordered so that $2\rhd1$, cellular basis $c_{11}:=1$ in cell $1$ and $c_{22}:=x$ in cell $2$ and $i=\mathrm{id}$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). The cell form on $C^{2}$ has $c_{22}c_{22}=x^2=0$, so it is identically zero, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{2}=C^{2}$ and $D^{2}=0$, while both $C^{1}$ and $C^{2}$ are one-dimensional simple modules: on either, $a+bx$ acts as the scalar $a$. In particular the Jacobson radical of $C^{2}$ is zero and its actual head is $C^{2}$, even though its cell-form radical is all of $C^{2}$ and its cell-form quotient is zero: cellularity does not force $D^{\lambda}\ne0$, and the algebra is not semisimple since $\mathrm{rad}\,A=(x)$.

(b) Hecke instance: let $F$ be a field of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)=2$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); for $n=3$ and $\lambda=(1,1,1)$ the partition $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]), so $D^{(1,1,1)}=0$ while the page's Specht module $S^{(1,1,1)}\cong D^{(3)}$ is the nonzero trivial module (in characteristic $2$ the sign module is trivial) ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

(c) Reducible cell module: in the $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$, $e=2$ specialization of the example the q-Schur cell module $W^{(3,2)}_F$ satisfies $\sum_{i>0}[W^{(3,2)}_F(i)]=[L^{(3,1^2)}_F]+2[L^{(2^2,1)}_F]\ne0$ ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], the calculation of [[ex-q-schaper-for-shape-three-two-at-e-two]]), so its radical is nonzero and $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is reducible even though it has a simple head.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The three settings above: the algebra $A=F[x]/(x^2)$, the Hecke algebra $H_{F,q}(S_3)$ in characteristic $2$ at $q=1$, and the q-Schur Weyl module $W^{(3,2)}_F$ over $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$, at $e=2$.

[F1] ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]], [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]) For a cellular basis, products of two elements of the smaller cell vanish modulo the larger cell exactly when the corresponding form entry vanishes; $D^{\lambda}=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is zero if and only if the cell form is identically zero, and only in the nonzero case is $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ the module-theoretic Jacobson radical and the head quotient.

[F2] ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]], [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]) For $F$ of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$ the quantum characteristic is $e=2$, $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular, and $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ exactly for the $e$-regular $\lambda$.

[F3] ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], [[ex-q-schaper-for-shape-three-two-at-e-two]]) For the specified $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$ lift with $e=2$, the positive Jantzen submodule sum for $W^{(3,2)}_F$ is $[L^{(3,1^2)}_F]+2[L^{(2^2,1)}_F]\ne0$.




## Counterexample

1.1 The abstract instance: in $A=F[x]/(x^2)$ with $c_{11}=1$, $c_{22}=x$ and $2\rhd1$, the product $c_{22}c_{22}=x^2=0$ is congruent to $0\cdot c_{22}$ modulo $A^{\rhd2}=0$, so the axiom holds with zero form value; the products $c_{11}(a+bx)=a+bx\equiv a\,c_{11}\pmod{(x)}$ and $c_{22}(a+bx)=ax=a\,c_{22}$ confirm the triangularity. Hence $C^{2}$ has identically zero form, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{2}=C^{2}$ and $D^{2}=0$; the module $C^{2}$ itself is one-dimensional with $a+bx$ acting as $a$, hence simple with zero Jacobson radical and head $C^{2}\ne0$. Moreover $x\in A$ is a nonzero nilpotent, so $\mathrm{rad}\,A=(x)\ne0$ and $A$ is not semisimple. [given, F1]

1.2 The Hecke instance: for $F$ of characteristic $2$ and $q=1$ the sign module is the trivial module, so the Murphy cell module $S^{(3)}_{\mathrm M}$ and its theta-pullback $S^{(1,1,1)}=(S^{(3)}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ are the trivial module; the label $(1,1,1)$ is not $2$-regular, so by [F2] $D^{(1,1,1)}=0$ while $S^{(1,1,1)}\ne0$. [given, F2]

1.3 The reducible Weyl module. In the precise lift of [F3], the sum of the positive filtration-submodule classes is $[L^{(3,1^2)}]+2[L^{(2,2,1)}]\ne0$. At least one of these submodules is nonzero. Since all are contained in the first reduced submodule $W_F(1)=\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}W_F$, that radical is nonzero. The Schur cell form has nonzero simple head, so its form radical is its unique maximal proper submodule. Consequently $W_F^{(3,2)}$ is reducible, despite having simple head $L^{(3,2)}$. The reduced form radical is not identified with $F\otimes_R$ the generic radical: specialization need not commute with this kernel, and the lifted generic form here is nondegenerate. [given, F1, F3]

2.1 Conclusion: the three instances refute the claims that cellularity forces semisimplicity, forces every cell module to be simple, or forces every labelled cell-form quotient to be nonzero; each is an application of the classification of cell-form quotients [F1] together with the explicit degenerate data. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, F1] ∎
