before_object.title: The Schur functor compares first-level branching with Hecke restriction
before_object.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^\times$, $\ell$ the quantum characteristic of $q$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and
$n\ge r$. Let $S(n,r)$ be the type-A q-Schur algebra with the idempotent $e$
of the weight $(1^r)$, so that $eS(n,r)e\cong H(r)$, and let
$f_{n,r}:S(n,r)\text{-mod}\to H(r)\text{-mod}$, $V\mapsto eV$, be the exact
Schur functor with left adjoint $h_{n,r}$
([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]). Let
$L_n(\lambda)$ be the irreducible $S(n,r)$-module for an $\ell$-restricted
$\lambda\vdash r$
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]), and let
$L_n(\lambda)^1$ be its first level, the sum of the weight spaces
$L_n(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha_i}$ over the simple roots, which is naturally an
$S(n-1,r-1)$-module. Then

1. $f_{n-1,r-1}\bigl(L_n(\lambda)^1\bigr)=f_{n,r}\bigl(L_n(\lambda)\bigr)
   \bigl\downarrow_{H(r-1)}$ as $H(r-1)$-modules, naturally in the pair
   $(n,r)$;
2. for $S(n,r)$-modules $W,V$ with $W^{(e)}=W$ and $V_{(e)}=0$ one has
   $\operatorname{Hom}_{S(n,r)}(W,V)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{H(r)}(fW,fV)$,
   so the functor detects and preserves the relevant Hom spaces and, being
   exact, transfers composition multiplicities of first-level modules;
3. if $\lambda$ is $\ell$-restricted, then the socle of the restriction of
   $L_n(\lambda)^1$ to the Levi subalgebra $U(n-1)$ consists of
   $\ell$-restricted labels.

At $q=1$ (so $\ell=p$ in characteristic $p$; characteristic zero gives
$\ell=\infty$) the specialization $H(r)\to kS_r$ of
([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]])
makes (i)-(iii) statements about $kS_r$-modules and the simple $kS_{r-1}$-modules
of
[[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]].

after_object.title: The Schur functor compares first-level branching with Hecke restriction
after_object.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^\times$, $\ell=e(F,q)$, and $n\ge r\ge1$; at the empty lower-rank boundary put $S(0,0)=H(0)=F$ with its identity functor. Use the left-module version of the q-Schur algebra $S(n,r)$ and its exact Schur functor $f_{n,r}:V\mapsto eV$ with left adjoint $h_{n,r}:X\mapsto S(n,r)e\otimes_{eS(n,r)e}X$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]). Right-module suppliers are converted to left modules through their star anti-involutions. All Specht and simple labels below are **Murphy labels**: $f(W^\mu)=S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $f(L_n(\mu))=D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, the latter nonzero exactly when $\mu$ is $\ell$-restricted ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

For a degree-$r$ polynomial module $V=\bigoplus_{|\alpha|=r}V_\alpha$, its **first level** is $$V^1:=\bigoplus_{\alpha_n=1}V_\alpha.$$ It is a module for the Levi polynomial algebra $S(n-1,r-1)$: the first $n-1$ coordinates sum to $r-1$. It is not the sum of the weights one simple root below the highest weight. For an $\ell$-restricted partition $\lambda\vdash r$, the following hold.

1. There is a natural $H(r-1)$-module isomorphism $$f_{n-1,r-1}(L_n(\lambda)^1)\cong      \operatorname{Res}_{H(r-1)}^{H(r)}f_{n,r}(L_n(\lambda)).$$ 2. For any $S(n,r)$-modules $W,V$ with $W^{(e)}=W$ and $V_{(e)}=0$, the Schur functor induces $$\operatorname{Hom}_{S(n,r)}(W,V)\cong      \operatorname{Hom}_{H(r)}(fW,fV).$$ Here $W^{(e)}=S(n,r)eW$ is the intersection of submodules whose quotient is killed by $e$, and $V_{(e)}$ is the sum of submodules killed by $e$. 3. The socle of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ as a Levi module has only $\ell$-restricted labels.

For every partition $\mu\vdash r-1$ with $\mu$ $\ell$-restricted, $$[L_n(\lambda)^1:L_{n-1}(\mu)]  =[\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}:D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}].$$ The exact functor transfers these surviving multiplicities; it may kill nonrestricted simple factors. At $q=1$ these statements hold over every field for the group algebras. In ordinary James labels the dictionary is $D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}\cong D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, not an untwisted identification with $D^\lambda$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).

For any $S(n,r)$-modules $W,V$ with $W^{(e)}=W$ and $V_{(e)}=0$, the Schur functor induces $$\operatorname{Hom}_{S(n,r)}(W,V)\cong      \operatorname{Hom}_{H(r)}(fW,fV).$$ Here $W^{(e)}=S(n,r)eW$ is the intersection of submodules whose quotient is killed by $e$, and $V_{(e)}$ is the sum of submodules killed by $e$. 3. The socle of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ as a Levi module has only $\ell$-restricted labels.

For every partition $\mu\vdash r-1$ with $\mu$ $\ell$-restricted, $$[L_n(\lambda)^1:L_{n-1}(\mu)]  =[\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}:D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}].$$ The exact functor transfers these surviving multiplicities; it may kill nonrestricted simple factors. At $q=1$ these statements hold over every field for the group algebras. In ordinary James labels the dictionary is $D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}\cong D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, not an untwisted identification with $D^\lambda$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, ranks, polynomial weight decomposition, and q-Schur and Hecke algebras of the Statement.

[F1] The permutation-summand realization is $S(n,r)=\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(\bigoplus_\alpha M^\alpha)$, with weight projections $1_\alpha$. The regular summand for a composition with exactly $r$ entries equal to $1$ is $M^\alpha=H(r)$. The standard corner is $\omega=(1^r,0^{n-r})$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]).

[F2] The exact Schur functor sends $W^\mu$ to $S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $L_n(\mu)$ to $D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, allowing zero images. The nonzero images have restricted labels and are pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F3] Brundan, full author manuscript, §3.22 defines polynomial levels by last-coordinate weight, using both $K_n$ and its binomial operators so the integer weight is determined even at a root of unity. The Levi $U(n-1)$ commutes with these operators. The q-Schur polynomial realization is the corresponding finite-degree quotient. In §5.5 the functors are left-module functors; star converts the right-module suppliers to this convention.

[F4] Brundan's Theorem 5.4 identifies the Levi socle of the first level with $\bigoplus_{i\in R^{\mathrm{good}}(\lambda)}L_{n-1}(\lambda(i))$; Lemma 5.7 proves these labels restricted when $\lambda$ is restricted. These are the source's intrinsic good-node labels, not an identification of cellular and crystal labels. This input is used only for assertion 3. Its full relevant proof (§5.3-5.7, printed pp. 29-32) was consulted; a new local construction of all lowering-operator theory in the preceding sections is not claimed.

[F5] At $q=1$ the actual ordinary polytabloid/signed-conjugate Murphy comparison gives the group module dictionary, with form factor $1$, over every field. It follows through the corrected Definition and the actual NEW50 comparison and specialization suppliers, not the printed-page-25 untwisted warning ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Construct the lower-rank action directly over the given field. Put $M_0=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Lambda(n-1,r-1)}M^\alpha$ for $H(r-1)$. Length-additive parabolic coset bases give $M^{(\alpha,1)}\cong M^\alpha\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ by $x_\alpha h\otimes a\mapsto x_\alpha ha$. Thus the summands with last coordinate $1$ form $M_1\cong M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$. The functorial algebra homomorphism $f\mapsto f\otimes1$ embeds $S(n-1,r-1)$ into $\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(M_1)$: the Hecke algebra $H(r)$ is free on its parabolic coset basis and contains the unit coset, so the map is injective. Extend these maps by zero to the remaining summands of $M$ and put $p=\sum_{\alpha_n=1}1_\alpha$. For every left $S(n,r)$-module $V$, $V^1=pV$ is therefore a natural $S(n-1,r-1)$-module. This supplies the lower-rank action without assuming that the first level is a sum of root-adjacent highest-weight spaces, and without adjoining a square root of the Hecke parameter. It agrees with the last-coordinate polynomial level of [F3]. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 Prove the Hom assertion algebraically. For $S=S(n,r)$ put $\overline W=Se\otimes_{eSe}eW$ and let $\varepsilon:\overline W\to W$ send $se\otimes w$ to $sw$. Its image is $SeW=W^{(e)}$, which is $W$ under the stated hypothesis. Applying $e$ identifies $e\varepsilon$ with the isomorphism $eSe\otimes_{eSe}eW\to eW$. Exactness of $e(-)$ therefore gives $eK=0$ for $K=\ker\varepsilon$. The exact sequence is $$0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow\overline W   \xrightarrow{\varepsilon}W\longrightarrow0.$$ For any $S$-map $g:\overline W\to V$, its image $g(K)$ is an $S$-submodule killed by $e$, so it is contained in $V_{(e)}=0$. Thus $g$ factors uniquely through $W$. The adjunction then gives $\operatorname{Hom}_H(eW,eV)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(\overline W,V) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(W,V)$. This proves assertion 2, with the kernel and quotient in the correct direction. [given, F1]

2.1 Reconcile the corners for all $n\ge r$. Put $\omega_*=(1^{r-1},0^{n-r},1)$ and $e_*=1_{\omega_*}$. Both $M^\omega$ and $M^{\omega_*}$ are the regular module $H(r)$. Their fixed identity isomorphism gives block matrix units $u,v\in S(n,r)$ with $u=e_*ue$, $v=eve_*$, $uv=e_*$ and $vu=e$. Thus multiplication by $u$ gives a natural isomorphism $eV\to e_*V$, with inverse multiplication by $v$, and carries the standard regular corner action to the $e_*$ corner action. When $n=r$ these corners coincide. This explicitly supplies the natural corner identification instead of treating an idempotent with last coordinate $0$ as lying in the first level. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 The restricted-socle assertion is Brundan's Lemma 5.7. By [F4] every socle label is $\lambda(i)$ for a good row $i$. If it were not restricted while $\lambda$ is restricted, then $i>1$ and $\lambda_{i-1}-\lambda_i=\ell-1$. The last nodes of rows $i-1$ and $i$ then have equal residue, and the source's normality criterion forces row $i-1$ to be normal, contradicting the minimality of the good row $i$ in that residue. Thus all socle labels are restricted. At $\ell=\infty$ all partitions are restricted. For the stable-rank boundary $n=r$ with $\lambda_n>0$, necessarily $\lambda=(1^r)$: the determinant module and its first level are one-dimensional determinant modules, and the conclusion holds directly. [F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Compute the first-level corner inside this induced action. The lower regular summand is $H(r-1)$, whose induction is $H(r-1)\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)=H(r)$, exactly the summand of type $\omega_*$. Its weight projection on $pV$ is $e_*$, so $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)=e_*V$. The lower corner operator given by left multiplication by $h\in H(r-1)$ induces left multiplication by the same $h$ on $H(r)$ under $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$. Thus every generator $T_1,\ldots,T_{r-2}$ acts exactly as its image in the upper regular corner, by equality of these explicit endomorphisms. The matrix units of step 2.1 identify the upper standard corner with this regular summand. They consequently give $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)\cong\operatorname{Res}f_{n,r}(V)$ on every module. This is an algebra-level calculation; it needs no generic semisimplicity or cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Transfer composition multiplicities by exactness, not by a Hom-space count. Apply $f_{n-1,r-1}$ to a finite composition series of $L_n(\lambda)^1$. By [F2] its factors become either zero or the pairwise nonisomorphic $D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}$ for restricted $\mu$. Removing repeated terms of the resulting filtration therefore preserves the number of each surviving simple factor. Step 3.1 identifies its result with $\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}$, proving the stated equality. Assertion 3 is not used to claim that every composition factor survives; a socle statement alone would not justify that claim. [F2, step 3.1]

5.1 At $q=1$, [F5] identifies the corner algebras with group algebras. In ordinary regular labels the two modules are simultaneously twisted by sign and both partition labels are conjugated. Sign restricts along the group tower, is exact, and preserves the two compared multiplicities. This is the ordinary group interpretation, including characteristic $2$; it is not an untwisted identification of a restricted label with the same regular label. Steps 3.1, 1.2, 2.2 and 4.1 prove all the assertions. [F5, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ (every field is splitting for symmetric groups, so no algebraic closedness is needed) and let $\lambda$ be a $p$-regular partition of $n$ ([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]), so that $D^\lambda$ is the simple head of the Specht module $S^\lambda_k$ ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). Let $A=(j,\lambda_j)$ be a removable node of $\lambda$ whose removal $\lambda(j)$ is again $p$-regular, and call $A$ **normal** for $\lambda$ when the transposed node $(\lambda_j,j)$ of the $p$-restricted partition $\lambda'$ is a normal node in the sense of [[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]] (this is Kleshchev's normality; it is computed in the reduced signature of the correct residue class of $\lambda'$). Then $$[\,D^\lambda{\downarrow}_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}\,]=0$$ if $A$ is not normal, and $$[\,D^\lambda{\downarrow}_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}\,]=1+\#\{B:\ B\ \text{is a normal removable node of }\lambda\text{ strictly above }A\text{ with }\operatorname{res}(B)=\operatorname{res}(A)\}$$ if $A$ is normal. Here $\operatorname{res}$ is the residue $c-r\bmod p$ and "above" means strictly smaller row index. Equivalently, the multiplicity is the first-level multiplicity $\gamma(A)$ of Kleshchev 1997, so it is the number of normal nodes of $\lambda$ weakly above $A$ in $A$'s residue class, and $A$ is normal precisely when this number is nonzero.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$, a $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$ and a removable node $A=(j,\lambda_j)$ with $\lambda(j)$ $p$-regular.

[F1] The residue-summand decomposition of the restriction and the dictionary between the $p$-regular and the $p$-restricted labels: $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ for $p$-restricted $\mu$, and the transposed node dictionary of Brundan Remark 2.4(II) translates normality of a removable node of $\lambda$ into normality of the transposed node of $\lambda'$ in the signature sense of [[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]] ([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]).

[F2] Apply the corrected Schur-functor comparison to the **restricted** partition $\mu=\lambda'$, and to $\nu=\lambda(j)'$ at the lower degree. For a stable Schur rank $N\ge n$, its first level consists of polynomial weights with last coordinate $1$. The comparison and exactness give $$[L_N(\mu)^1:L_{N-1}(\nu)]   =[\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}:D_{\mathrm M}^{\nu}].$$ At $q=1$, the actual signed-conjugate dictionary says $D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}\cong D^\lambda\otimes\operatorname{sgn}_n$ and $D_{\mathrm M}^{\nu}\cong D^{\lambda(j)}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}_{n-1}$. Since sign restricts to sign, twisting **both** modules leaves the multiplicity unchanged. This proves the precise group-to-first-level transfer used below ([[prop-schur-functor-compares-first-level-branching-with-hecke-restriction]], [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]). No Schur functor is applied to the ordinary regular label $\lambda$ as if it were restricted.

[F3] The source's algebraic-group count is indexed by dominant weights, not by the characteristic as a rank. In Kleshchev §11 take $N=n$, $l=N-1$, and let $w_n(\lambda)$ be the type-$A_l$ dominant weight whose fundamental-weight coefficients are $\lambda'_a-\lambda'_{a+1}$. It is the weight underlying the polynomial highest weight $\mu=\lambda'$. The lower label is $w_{n-1}(\lambda(j))$, and for $\lambda\ne(n)$ $$w_{n-1}(\lambda(j))=\operatorname{res}_{A_{l-1}}    \bigl(w_n(\lambda)-\alpha(\lambda_j,l)\bigr).$$ Theorem 9.3 computes the corresponding multiplicity in the first level restricted to $A_{l-1}$; §11, Proposition 11.2 and the deduction on printed pp. 64-65 identify this count with the one at the removed ordinary node. The index is the column $\lambda_j$ after conjugation, not the ordinary row $j$ treated as an unchanged Schur label. The combinatorial recurrence and basis results of Part I/II remain the recorded source inputs; their full local reconstruction is not claimed by this binding repair. For $\lambda=(n)$ the ordinary module is trivial and its sole removable-node multiplicity is $1$, handled directly. The case $n=1$ is the trivial restriction to $S_0$. Neither $A_{p-1}$ nor a rank determined by the characteristic is used.

[F4] Kleshchev 1997, Theorem 1.4 and its reformulation (manuscript p. 5), together with Corollary 5.8(ii) (manuscript p. 44) and the index identities $\lambda_k-\lambda_j+j-k+1=B_{w_n(\lambda)}(\lambda_j,\lambda_k)$ and $\lambda_k-\lambda_j+j-k=C_{w_n(\lambda)}(\lambda_j,\lambda_k)$ used on manuscript pp. 64-65: the corresponding root-indexed count $\gamma_{w_n(\lambda)}(\lambda_j,l)$ of [F3] equals $1$ plus the number of normal nodes of $\lambda$ strictly above $A$ in the same residue class when $A$ is normal, and is $0$ when $A$ is not normal.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Reduction to the correctly labelled first level. Put $\mu=\lambda'$ and $\nu=\lambda(j)'$. These are $p$-restricted because both ordinary labels are $p$-regular. By [F2], the exact first-level comparison identifies the multiplicity of $L_{N-1}(\nu)$ in $L_N(\mu)^1$ with the multiplicity of $D_{\mathrm M}^{\nu}$ in $\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}$. At $q=1$, twist both compared modules by sign, which restricts along $S_{n-1}\subset S_n$, and use the conjugate-label dictionary. This yields exactly $[D^\lambda\downarrow_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}]$. The algebraic weight and removed-root indexing are those of [F3]. In particular neither the ordinary regular label itself nor the characteristic is substituted for a Schur label or algebraic-group rank. [given, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 The first-level multiplicity is the combinatorial count. By the theorem recorded in [F3], the corresponding first-level multiplicity at the transposed removed node, indexed as in [F3], is the integer $\gamma_{w_n(\lambda)}(\lambda_j,l)$ of the source's first-level recurrence, which is computed by the recurrence recorded in [F3]; no Fock-space or Ariki input is used. [step 1.1, F3]

3.1 Identification of the count. By the results recorded in [F4], the count $\gamma_{w_n(\lambda)}(\lambda_j,l)$ is $0$ when $A$ is not normal and equals $1+\#\{B:B\text{ normal removable node of }\lambda\text{ strictly above }A,\ \operatorname{res}(B)=\operatorname{res}(A)\}$ when $A$ is normal; the two expressions of the statement both describe this integer, and the normality of $A$ is read in the reduced signature of $\lambda'$ via the transposed-node dictionary of [F1]. [step 2.1, F1, F4]

4.1 Calibration with the source's worked example. For $p=3$ and $\lambda=(5,3,2)$ the removable nodes are $(1,5)$, $(2,3)$, $(3,2)$ with residues $5-1=4\equiv1$, $3-2\equiv1$, $2-3\equiv2$; transposing gives $\lambda'=(3,3,2,1,1)$, in which the nodes $(3,2),(5,1)$ and no further node form the normal $2$-class, so the normal nodes of $\lambda$ are $(2,3)$ and $(1,5)$, and the formula gives multiplicities $2$ (for $(2,3)$, with one normal node above it) and $1$ (for $(1,5)$); the node $(3,2)$ is not normal and contributes $0$. This reproduces the multiplicities $1,2,0$ recorded in the source (manuscript p. 5) for the nodes $(1,5),(2,3),(3,2)$. [step 3.1, F1, F4]

5.1 Conclusion. Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 give $[D^\lambda\downarrow_{S_{n-1}}:D^{\lambda(j)}]=0$ for non-normal $A$ and the displayed count for normal $A$, and step 4.1 checks the normalization against the source's example. The reduction of step 1.1 uses only the $q=1$ specialization of the Schur-functor comparison; the combinatorial inputs [F3] and [F4] are the recorded content of Kleshchev 1997, whose Part I/II arguments are cited by exact locators and not replaced by a weaker statement. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

before_object.title: q-Schur Weyl modules are in the same block iff their labels have the same e-core
before_object.statement: Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]), let $d\ge n$, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl modules of $S_F(d,n)$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then for partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S_F(d,n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $S_F(d,n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. (For $e=\infty$ every partition is its own core and every Weyl module is its own block, the algebra being semisimple.)

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]), let $d\ge n$, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl modules of $S_F(d,n)$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then for partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S_F(d,n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $S_F(d,n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. (For $e=\infty$ every partition is its own core and every Weyl module is its own block, the algebra being semisimple.)

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, parameter $q$, quantum characteristic $e$, integer $d\ge n$, and the Weyl modules in the statement. Write $S=S_F(d,n)$ and $W^{\lambda}=W^{\lambda}_F$.

[F1] The semistandard cellular basis has cells $W^{\lambda}$, nonzero absolutely simple heads $L^{\lambda}$, and dominance-unitriangular decomposition multiplicities $d_{\lambda\mu}$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The cellular anti-involution induces contragredient duality fixing the simple isomorphism classes, through the nondegenerate cell form on each simple head ([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]], [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]).

[F2] The balanced hook-ratio Jantzen formula and alternating beta symbols ([[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]], [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]) use conjugate beta numbers $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+N-j$, with $N$ sufficiently large, and read $$\sum_{r>0}[W^{\lambda}(r)]=\sum_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],\ b<c}\bigl(v(h^{\lambda}_{ab})-v(h^{\lambda}_{ac})\bigr)[W^{\beta+h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_b-h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_c}],$$ where $W^{\lambda}(r)$ are filtration submodules, $W^{\lambda}(1)=\operatorname{rad}W^{\lambda}$, and the right hand symbols are zero on repeated or negative entries and otherwise have the sign of sorting the beta sequence. The suppliers must carry this balanced form; the earlier displayed unbalanced manuscript indices do not preserve degree.

[F3] Core abaci are obtained by packing beads upwards on each runner, so their shapes depend only on runner bead counts; rim-hook removal is a bead-to-gap move ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Conjugation reverses dominance ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]).

[F4] Primitive central idempotents decompose the identity, and every finite-dimensional module splits into their block summands ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]). Weyl classes are linearly independent in the Grothendieck group, so a nonzero accumulated Weyl coefficient in the class of a module supported in one block forces that Weyl module into the block ([[lem-virtual-weyl-combinations-detect-q-schur-block-separation]], [[lem-semistandard-weight-dimensions-detect-virtual-weyl-classes]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Lift and valuation. Use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ with $\hat q=X$ and uniformizer $X-q$. The element $X$ is a unit since $q\ne0$, and every polynomial $[m]_X=1+X+\cdots+X^{m-1}$ is nonzero, so the generic factorial is nonzero. Its valuation $v(m)$ is positive exactly when $[m]_q=0$, equivalently $e\mid m$ for finite $e$; for $e=\infty$ all valuations vanish. In characteristic $p$ the positive valuation may exceed1, which causes no difficulty below. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 Block support and Jantzen edges. A finite-dimensional module with simple head is indecomposable: every nonzero summand has nonzero head, so two summands would make the head nonsimple. Thus $W^{\lambda}$ has just one nonzero block summand, and every Jantzen submodule is supported in that block. By [F4], any nonzero accumulated coefficient $J_{\lambda\mu}$ of $[W^{\mu}]$ in [F2] puts $W^{\lambda},W^{\mu}$ in the same block. This uses the sum of submodule classes, without identifying it with the radical class. [F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Balanced terms preserve the core and descend in dominance. Put $s=h_{ab}$ and $t=h_{ac}$, so $s-t=\beta_b-\beta_c$. If a hook coefficient is nonzero, at least one of $s,t$ is divisible by $e$. If $e\mid t$, the shifted bead residues are unchanged. Otherwise $e\mid s$, so $t\equiv\beta_c-\beta_b\pmod e$ and the two shifted residues exchange. Thus every surviving symbol has the same runner counts and core as $\lambda$. Moreover replacing the two conjugate beta entries $u>v$ by $u+t,v-t$ strictly increases conjugate majorization; the sorted target therefore strictly decreases original dominance. Accumulating equal target labels preserves both conclusions. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 No outgoing edge implies a binary row condition. Suppose every accumulated outgoing coefficient from $\mu$ is zero. For row $i$, put $g_i=N+i-1-\mu_i$, a gap in its conjugate beta set; its row hooks are exactly $\beta_j-g_i>0$. If that row contained a divisible hook $s$ and a nondivisible hook $t$, repeatedly replace $t$ by $s+t$ while their sum is another row hook. This finite climb ends with $s+t$ absent from the hook set. The balanced term for the nodes of hook lengths $s,t$ then has lower shifted bead $g_i$, which is a gap, and upper shifted bead $g_i+s+t$, which is absent from the beta set. Its symbol survives and its coefficient is $\pm v(s)\ne0$. There is no cancellation: any surviving balanced term replaces two lost values by a new value larger than both and a new value smaller than both, so those four values determine the pair and its row gap uniquely; the gaps $g_i$ strictly increase with $i$. This contradicts the zero accumulated coefficient. Therefore each row has either all hook lengths divisible by $e$ or none; call this the binary row condition. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Composition-factor cores. An off-head simple occurs in $W^{\lambda}$ exactly when it occurs in its radical, equivalently in the positive Jantzen sum: the first submodule is the radical and every later one is contained in it. Its nonzero multiplicity in that sum implies it occurs in some $W^{\mu}$ with $J_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$, since otherwise its coefficient in the sum would be zero. Step 2.1 gives the same core and strict dominance descent. Induction on the finite dominance poset proves that every factor $L^{\nu}$ of $W^{\lambda}$ has $C_e(\nu)=C_e(\lambda)$. No identity equating the radical class with the positive sum is asserted. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Vertical core removal under the binary row condition. A removable $e$-hook has hook length $e$ at its defining node. Every hook in that row is then divisible, so its last-column hook, a positive multiple of $e$ no larger than $e$, equals $e$. Hook lengths strictly decrease across the row, forcing the defining node to be at the row end: the strip is vertical on $e$ equal-length rows $i,\ldots,i+e-1$ in column $j$. Removing it decreases that column height by $e$. In unaffected rows hook divisibility is unchanged. For an affected row $i+t$, hooks in the retained columns were all congruent to $-t$ modulo $e$, because row $i$ had all hooks divisible and those rows had equal length. Their new hook lengths are all congruent to $-t-1$, so the binary row condition persists. Induction shows every core-removal strip is vertical. [F3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The Cartan graph locally. Choose a complete orthogonal primitive idempotent system of $S$, with one representative $f_\mu$ for each simple label and repeated representatives as necessary. Such a system lifts matrix diagonal idempotents from the split semisimple quotient: the radical is nilpotent and the iteration $u\mapsto u+(1-2u)(u^2-u)$ squares the idempotency error, so finite iteration lifts an idempotent; successively working in complementary corners lifts an orthogonal system. Absolute simplicity gives $\dim L^{\lambda}f_\mu=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$, hence exact multiplication by $f_\mu$ gives $\dim W^{\lambda}f_\mu=d_{\lambda\mu}$. The successive cellular ideal bimodules are the contragredient cell module tensor the right cell module. Apply the exact projection $f_\mu(-)f_\nu$ and add their dimensions; [F1]'s duality fixes the simple labels, giving $\dim f_\mu Sf_\nu=\sum_\lambda d_{\lambda\mu}d_{\lambda\nu}$. This is the Cartan entry of the primitive projective $f_\mu S$. A disconnected graph on the full primitive idempotent system, with edges whenever either mixed corner is nonzero, yields central idempotents by summing each component: all mixed corners vanish in both directions. Conversely a central block idempotent forbids mixed corners. Thus simple labels in one block are joined by pairs sharing a Weyl factor, and step 3.1 proves that labels in the same block have the same core. [F1, F4, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 The minimum label and the bridge shapes. Fix core $\gamma$ and weight $w$, and set $\rho=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_l,1^{ew})$. It has core $\gamma$ by removing its bottom vertical $e$-strips, and is dominance-minimal in the class: every same-core partition contains $\gamma$ as a diagram, and appending all additional boxes as rows of size1 minimizes each dominance partial sum. Let $\mu\ne\rho$ satisfy the binary row condition. Choose the first row $i$ with divisible hooks and put $j=\mu_i$, $h=h^{\mu}_{ij}=\mu'_j-i+1$, a positive multiple of $e$. If $j=1$, every divisible hook is in column1, so step 3.2 would give $\mu=\rho$; thus $j>1$. Remove the vertical $h$-strip, obtaining $\sigma$, then add $h$ boxes horizontally to its first row to get $\nu$, and vertically to its first column to get $\eta$. All have the same core, since $h$ is a multiple of $e$; $\nu$ dominates $\mu,\eta$, and $\eta$ is strictly below $\mu$ because the removed nodes are moved into new bottom rows. [F3, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 The bridge coefficients are nonzero. Write $l=\ell(\mu)=\ell(\sigma)$. If $i>1$, then $\sigma_1=\mu_1$ and the row1 hook pair in $\nu$ at columns $j,\mu_1+1$ has lengths $A=h^{\mu}_{1j}$ and $h$: the first is nondivisible because row1 precedes the first divisible row, and the second is divisible. Its balanced symbol sorts to $\mu$, so its coefficient is nonzero. If $i=1$, then $\sigma_1=j-1$, and the row1 pair at columns $j,j+1$ has lengths $h,h-1$; its balanced transfer $h-1$ sorts to $\mu$, again giving a nonzero coefficient. For $\eta$, the pair at columns $1,\sigma_1+1$ has lengths $A'=\sigma_1+h+l-1$ and $h$. When $i>1$, $A'-h^{\mu}_{i1}=A$, so $A'$ is nondivisible; when $i=1$, $A'=h^{\mu}_{11}+h-1$, also nondivisible. Its balanced symbol sorts to $\eta$. Each claimed target has precisely two lost and two gained beta values, so the uniqueness argument in step 2.2 rules out cancellation. Thus both $J_{\nu\mu}$ and $J_{\nu\eta}$ are nonzero. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Connectivity and sufficiency. Induct upwards from $\rho$ in the finite dominance poset. For $\mu\ne\rho$, if an outgoing coefficient $J_{\mu\tau}$ is nonzero, then $\tau$ is strictly below $\mu$ in the same core class by step 2.1, so induction connects $\tau$, and hence $\mu$, to $\rho$. If no outgoing coefficient exists, steps 2.2, 3.2, 4.2 and 5.1 connect $\mu$ to $\nu$ and then $\eta$, with $\eta$ strictly below $\mu$, and induction again connects it to $\rho$. Every such edge is a same-block implication by step 1.2. Thus every pair of labels of the same core lies in the same block. Together with step 4.1 this proves the equivalence. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Parameterization and infinite characteristic. Every simple is the head of a Weyl module, so every block has a partition label. The core sizes are $n-ew$, and each admissible core occurs via the partition $\rho$ of step 4.2; step 6.1 therefore gives the stated indexing. If $e=\infty$, all coefficients vanish by step 1.1, so positivity forces every first Jantzen submodule, hence every radical, to vanish. All Weyl modules are simple; their decomposition matrix is the identity. Step 4.1 then gives identity Cartan matrix, so every primitive projective is simple and $S$ is semisimple, with each partition its own block and core. This proves all assertions. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 6.1] ∎

The connectivity argument follows the corrected dominance-minimum route of Lyle–Mathas Proposition 3.7 and Corollary 4.3, while proving the needed elementary row properties locally. Their final Remark explicitly corrects the earlier first-row-only q-Schur argument; the old direct hook move can have zero coefficient.

[F1] Each Weyl module has simple head $L^{\lambda}$ of multiplicity one, the decomposition matrix is dominance-unitriangular, and all simple modules are obtained this way ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). In a finite-dimensional module, a simple head implies indecomposability: any nonzero direct summand has a nonzero head, so two nonzero summands would give a nonsimple head.

This is the balanced hook-ratio formula required from [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] and [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. Its source arithmetic must be repaired before binding: the manuscript's displayed beta indices are inconsistent, while its worked Example 5.28 determines the balanced transfer.

The bead move removes/adds a rim $e$-hook, and distinct runners give distinct partitions ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). The ordinary Specht dictionary uses conjugation and the same $\theta$ pullback on every module ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Enumeration and ordering. Choose a conjugate core beta set long enough that every runner contains a bead, and list its bottom beads $x_1<\cdots<x_e$. Each runner is packed, so replacing $x_k$ by $x_k+e$ gives precisely the $e$ weight-one partitions, denoted $\lambda_k$. For $j>k$, moving $x_j$ instead of $x_k$ gives the more dominant conjugate partition: comparing the sorted bead lists, each partial sum increases when the move starts at the larger bead. Conjugation reverses dominance, hence $\lambda_1\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. The largest original partition is $(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$, since its added horizontal first-row strip dominates every other placement. [F3, construct, algebra]

1.2 Choose a lift with valuation one. If $q\ne1$, its finite quantum characteristic $e$ is its multiplicative order, and is prime to the field characteristic; use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ and $\hat q=X$. The derivative of $X^e-1$ at $q$ is $eq^{e-1}\ne0$, so $\nu([e]_X)=1$; also $\nu([h]_X)=0$ when $e\nmid h$. If $q=1$, then $\operatorname{char}F=p=e$. First work over $\mathbb F_p$ with $R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, $\hat q=1$, giving $\nu([e]_1)=\nu(p)=1$ and $\nu([h]_1)=0$ for $p\nmid h$, and then extend scalars to $F$. This extension preserves the decomposition multiplicities because the q-Schur simple modules are absolutely irreducible and its integral Weyl modules commute with scalar extension. In both cases the generic factorial is nonzero and [F2] applies. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Restriction. If $\lambda$ is not restricted, some $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}\ge e$, so removing the last $e$ boxes of row $i$ leaves a partition. Its size is $|\gamma|$ and its core is $\gamma$, so it equals $\gamma$. Thus $\lambda$ is obtained by adding $e$ boxes to row $i$ of $\gamma$. An $e$-core has $\gamma_r-\gamma_{r+1}<e$ for every $r$, since otherwise it has a removable horizontal $e$-strip. Consequently $i>1$ is impossible: the partition inequality $\gamma_{i-1}\ge\gamma_i+e$ would contradict this core property. Therefore the only nonrestricted member is $\lambda_1=(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$; it is indeed nonrestricted because its first-row difference is at least $e$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Evaluate the balanced formula. A nonzero coefficient involves a hook of length divisible by $e$. A weight-one abacus has exactly one bead-gap pair of equal residue with the gap below the bead: $x_k+e$ and $x_k$; thus its only $e$-divisible hook has length $e$. Any surviving term in [F2] replaces two bead values, and its new runner counts equal the old ones: either $e$ divides the transfer $h_{ac}$, leaving residues fixed, or $e$ divides $h_{ab}=h_{ac}+\beta_b-\beta_c$, exchanging their residues. Hence its sorted symbol is one of the $\lambda_j$. For $j>k$, the distinct bead sets of $\lambda_k$ and $\lambda_j$ differ exactly by replacing $x_k+e,x_j$ with $x_k,x_j+e$. There is exactly one balanced transfer yielding this change: if $x_j<x_k+e$, its two hook lengths are $h_{ab}=e$, $h_{ac}=x_j-x_k$; if $x_j>x_k+e$, they are $h_{ab}=x_j-x_k$, $h_{ac}=e$. The difference $x_j-x_k$ is not divisible by $e$ since bottom beads are on distinct runners. Thus the respective unsigned coefficients are $+1$ and $-1$ by step 1.2. Sorting gives in either case the signed coefficient $(-1)^{j-k+1}$: in the packed core set, exactly one bead from each runner with bottom bead $>x_r$ lies between $x_r$ and $x_r+e$, so moving $x_r$ crosses $e-r$ beads; the relative sorting parity for the two moves, together with their opposite orientation, is $(-1)^{(e-j)-(e-k)+1}$. There are no other terms and no repeated contributions: the two lost and two gained bead values determine the pair and transfer uniquely. Therefore $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=\sum_{j>k}(-1)^{j-k+1}[W^{\lambda_j}]$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Descending induction and the matrix. For $k=e$, step 2.2 gives zero on the left; all summands are actual submodule classes with nonnegative simple multiplicities, so $W^{\lambda_e}(1)=0$ and $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$. Suppose the stated rows are known for $j>k$. Substitution into step 2.2 telescopes to $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Since $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ and each later term is a submodule of $W(1)$, positivity shows $W(1)\cong L^{\lambda_{k+1}}$ and $W(i)=0$ for $i\ge2$. The head quotient is $L^{\lambda_k}$, giving $[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Notice that the identity $[W]=[L]+\sum_{i>0}[W(i)]$ is used only after proving all later filtration submodules vanish; it is false for a general Jantzen filtration. Reading simple multiplicities yields the complete $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix. [F1, F2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Specht rows. Apply the exact functor of [F4] to step 3.1 and use step 2.1: $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$, while the other $D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}$ are the nonzero simples. This gives exactly the three displayed Murphy Specht class identities, hence the full $e\times(e-1)$ Murphy matrix. Conjugation sends the core to $\gamma'$ and the restricted simple labels to regular ones, and the same $\theta$ pullback applied to every module preserves all composition multiplicities. Thus the ordinary Specht matrix has the same entries under the accepted conjugate/sign label dictionary. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), and let $S^{\lambda}$ be the type-A Hecke Specht module of this page in the Dipper-James convention ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) for $\lambda\vdash n$. Then for all partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ the modules $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Equivalently the blocks of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ of size at most $n$ with $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. (For $e=\infty$ the Hecke algebra is semisimple and each partition is its own core, so the statement is the trivial block decomposition.)

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$, a partition $n\ge0$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ with Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ for $\lambda\vdash n$, and a fixed integer $d\ge n$.

[F1] For $d\ge n$, the Schur idempotent $e\in S=S_F(d,n)$ satisfies $eSe\cong H$, and $X\mapsto Xe$ is exact. It sends each Weyl module $W^{\lambda}$ to the nonzero Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$; its simple images are zero or the Murphy simple modules, with the nonzero images indexed by the $e$-restricted partitions ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F2] Blocks: $1=\sum_D\delta_D$ is the unique decomposition of the identity of a finite-dimensional algebra into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents, blocks are the ideals cut out by the $\delta_D$, and every nonzero central idempotent is a sum of some of the $\delta_D$ ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]).

[F3] The q-Schur algebra and its Weyl modules: $S$ is finite-dimensional, $S=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for $M=\bigoplus_{\nu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\nu}$ with $M^{(1^n)}=H$, and $W^{\lambda}_F$ has head $L^{\lambda}_F$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

[F4] The q-Schur block theorem [[thm-q-schur-weyl-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]]: for $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F,W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S$ if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$; the blocks of $S$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$, $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$; and if $e=\infty$ then $S$ is semisimple with each $W^{\lambda}_F$ its own block.

[F5] The accepted ordinary/Murphy dictionary identifies the ordinary Specht module with the fixed $\theta$ pullback of the conjugate-shape Murphy cell module. Conjugation sends $C_e(\lambda)$ to $C_e(\lambda)'$, and sends restricted labels to regular labels. In particular it preserves equality of cores. An algebra automorphism permutes primitive central idempotents and therefore preserves the same-block relation ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Central idempotents of $H$ from blocks of $S$. For a block $C$ of $S$ with primitive central idempotent $\epsilon_C$ put $\tilde\epsilon_C:=\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Ce\in H$. This element is a central idempotent of $H$: it is idempotent because $\epsilon_C$ is, and for $x=ese\in H$ centrality of $\epsilon_C$ gives $x\tilde\epsilon_C=es\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Cse=\tilde\epsilon_Cx$; it is nonzero because it acts as the identity on the nonzero module $W^{\lambda}_Fe=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ for any $\lambda$ with $W^{\lambda}_F\in C$, namely $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\tilde\epsilon_C=W^{\lambda}_Fe\epsilon_Ce=W^{\lambda}_F\epsilon_Ce=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Moreover $\tilde\epsilon_C\tilde\epsilon_{C'}=e\epsilon_C\epsilon_{C'}e=0$ for $C\ne C'$ and $\sum_C\tilde\epsilon_C=e\sum_C\epsilon_Ce=e^2=1_H$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Number of q-Schur blocks is at least the number of Hecke blocks. Let $H=\bigoplus_iB_i$ be the block decomposition of $H$ with block identities $b_i$. Since $M=\bigoplus_{\nu}M^{\nu}$ and $H=M^{(1^n)}$ is a direct summand, $M=\bigoplus_iMb_i$ with each $Mb_i\ne0$ (it contains $Hb_i=B_i$), and $\mathrm{Hom}_H(Mb_i,Mb_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$, because a map $f$ satisfies $f(x)=f(xb_i)=f(x)b_i\in Mb_jb_i=0$. Hence $$S=\mathrm{End}_H(M)=\bigoplus_{i,j}\mathrm{Hom}_H(Mb_i,Mb_j)=\prod_i\mathrm{End}_H(Mb_i)$$ is a product of the nonzero algebras $\mathrm{End}_H(Mb_i)$, and a product of nonzero algebras has at least one block per factor; so $\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Number of Hecke blocks is at least the number of q-Schur blocks. Decompose each nonzero central idempotent $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 into primitive central idempotents of $H$ using the unique decomposition of $1_H$: every primitive central idempotent $\delta_D$ of $H$ with $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C=\delta_D$ belongs to exactly one $\tilde\epsilon_C$, because $\delta_D=\delta_D\cdot1_H=\sum_C\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C$ and pairwise orthogonality of the $\delta_D$ forces $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C\in\{0,\delta_D\}$. Since each $\tilde\epsilon_C\ne0$ has at least one such $\delta_D$, the blocks $D$ of $H$ are partitioned into nonempty supports over the blocks $C$ of $S$, and therefore $\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 A bijection of block sets, and the core criterion. By steps 2.1 and 1.2 the two block counts are equal, so each $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 has exactly one primitive summand and the map $C\mapsto\tilde\epsilon_C$ is a bijection from the blocks of $S$ onto the blocks of $H$. Since $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\lambda}_Fe$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\mu}_Fe$, the modules $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}$ lie in the same Hecke block if and only if $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same q-Schur block: indeed the block of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the image under the bijection of the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$. By the block theorem [F4] the latter holds if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$, which proves the q-Schur-normalised statement. [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 1.2]

4.1 Ordinary normalisation and semisimplicity. By [F5], $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block exactly when $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}$ do. Step 3.1 makes this equivalent to $C_e(\lambda')=C_e(\mu')$, and the identity $C_e(\nu')=C_e(\nu)'$ makes it equivalent to $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$. This identity follows by conjugating every removable border strip in a core-removal sequence; the terminal core also conjugates, by independence of removal order. For $e=\infty$, $S$ is semisimple by [F4]. Its corner $eSe$ is semisimple: in the Wedderburn decomposition of $S$, each idempotent selects a subspace in each matrix factor, and its corner is a product of matrix algebras over the same division rings. Thus $H\cong eSe$ is semisimple; the block bijection separates the partition labels. This proves all assertions. [F1, F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ (equivalently the residue field of the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, [[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]], [[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]) and let $n\ge0$. Two Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k,S^{\mu}_k$ of $k[S_n]$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ have the same $p$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $k[S_n]$ are indexed by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $\gamma$ a $p$-core, $w\in\mathbb N_0$ and $n=|\gamma|+pw$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$ with $w_p(\lambda)=(n-|C_p(\lambda)|)/p$ ([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A splitting field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$ with the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, an integer $n\ge0$, and the group algebra $k[S_n]$ with group Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k$ for $\lambda\vdash n$.

[F1] The algebra isomorphism $H_{k,1}(S_n)\cong k[S_n]$ sends each ordinary Dipper-James Specht module to the classical group Specht module of the same shape, and the quantum characteristic at $q=1$ in characteristic $p$ equals $p$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]], [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). The module comparison uses the accepted signed conjugate Murphy/ordinary dictionary before specialising; it does not identify the same-shape Murphy cell module with the ordinary Specht module.

[F2] The Hecke block criterion, in the Dipper-James normalisation of the same Specht modules as [F1]: [[cor-type-a-hecke-specht-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]] states that for a field $k$ and $q\in k^{\times}$ of quantum characteristic $e\ge2$, two Specht modules $S^{\lambda},S^{\mu}$ of $H_{k,q}(S_n)$ lie in the same block if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$, and that the blocks are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$.

[F4] The core-quotient size formula [[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]: for every $e\ge2$ and $\lambda\vdash n$ one has $n=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda)$ with $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|\in\mathbb N_0$, and for an $e$-core $\gamma$ the condition $|\gamma|\le n$, $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$ is exactly the condition that $n-|\gamma|$ be an admissible $e$-weight; conversely every such $\gamma$ occurs as the core of a partition of $n$ ([[thm-q-schur-weyl-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]).

[F5] An algebra isomorphism $\varphi:A\to B$ preserves blocks: it maps a central idempotent $z$ to the central idempotent $\varphi(z)$, preserves primitivity, and hence induces a bijection between the block sets ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]).

## Proof

 **Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Specialisation. Take $q=1\in k^{\times}$ and $e$ the quantum characteristic of $(k,q)$; since $q=1$ and $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$, [F1] gives $e=p$. By [F1] there is an algebra isomorphism $H_{k,1}(S_n)\cong k[S_n]$ carrying the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ to the group Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k$, so by [F5] this isomorphism induces a bijection between the blocks of the two algebras that matches $S^{\lambda}$ with $S^{\lambda}_k$; in particular $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if the corresponding Hecke Specht modules lie in the same block of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$. [F1, F5, algebra]

2.1 The core criterion. Applying the Hecke block criterion [F2] with $q=1$ and $e=p$, the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ lie in the same block if and only if the labels $\lambda,\mu$ have the same $p$-core. Together with step 1.1 this gives: $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $C_p(\lambda)=C_p(\mu)$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The parametrisation by cores and weights. By [F2] the blocks of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$, hence by step 1.1 the blocks of $k[S_n]$, are indexed by the $p$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod p$; the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ corresponds to $C_p(\lambda)$. For $n\ge0$ and such a $\gamma$ put $w:=(n-|\gamma|)/p\in\mathbb N_0$; by [F4] this is exactly the $p$-weight $w_p(\lambda)$ of any Specht label with core $\gamma$, and $n=|\gamma|+pw$. Since $w$ is determined by $n$ and $\gamma$, the map $\gamma\mapsto(\gamma,w)$ is a bijection onto the displayed set of pairs, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Steps 2.1 and 3.1 establish both assertions: the same-block criterion by the $p$-core, and the indexing of the blocks by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $n=|\gamma|+pw$ together with the identification of the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ as $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

The classification is stated independently, by a Young-module and Brauer-quotient route, as Theorem 1 of O'Donovan's preprint recorded in the sources; that reference is an independent confirmation of the statement and is not used in the proof above. No choice principle is used anywhere in this item.

before_object.statement: Take $e=p=3$ and the weight-one configuration $n=3$, $\gamma=\varnothing$ of [[thm-weight-one-block-decomposition-pattern]]; the three partitions of $3$ with $3$-core $\varnothing$ are $\lambda_1=(3)\rhd\lambda_2=(2,1)\rhd\lambda_3=(1,1,1)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). The associated q-Schur block at $p=3$ (with $d\ge3$) has the complete Weyl/simple decomposition matrix and with rows and columns in the order $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, equal to $\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$; applying the Schur functor and the conjugation/duality dictionary gives the Murphy Specht rows $[S^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]$, which in the page's $3$-regular labels $(3),(2,1)$ is the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ ([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]); the group-side entries are verified directly from the two-dimensional model $S^{(2,1)}$ of characteristic $3$, whose all-ones vector spans a trivial submodule with sign quotient, together with $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$ and $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$.
before_object.strategy: List the partitions of $3$ with $3$-core $\varnothing$: $(3)$ and $(1,1,1)$ remove their unique $3$-hook and $(2,1)$ removes its unique $3$-hook, giving exactly the three labels in the stated dominance order. Apply the weight-one theorem to obtain the bidiagonal Weyl matrix, then the Schur functor and the conjugation/duality dictionary $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^{\theta}$, $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^{\theta}$ to pass from the Murphy rows to the group-side matrix with rows and columns in the $p$-regular labels $(3),(2,1)$, and finally compare with the direct computation from the standard module: in characteristic $3$ the all-ones vector of $S^{(2,1)}$ spans a trivial submodule with sign quotient, so the rows of $S^{(3)},S^{(2,1)},S^{(1,1,1)}$ are $(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$ in the labels $(3),(2,1)$, and the simple labels are those of [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]. The two computations agree entry by entry, which is the verification of the example. No choice principle is used. Sources: Mathas, Proposition 5.38 and the accompanying discussion of $q=1$ (printed pp. 61-63); the published $S_3$ matrix.

after_object.statement:
Take $e=p=3$ and the weight-one configuration $n=3$, $\gamma=\varnothing$ of [[thm-weight-one-block-decomposition-pattern]]; the three partitions of $3$ with $3$-core $\varnothing$ are $\lambda_1=(3)\rhd\lambda_2=(2,1)\rhd\lambda_3=(1,1,1)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). The associated q-Schur weight-one class at $p=3$ (with $d\ge3$) has the complete Weyl/simple decomposition matrix, with rows and columns in the order $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, equal to $$\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$ Applying the Schur functor and the conjugation/duality dictionary gives the Murphy Specht rows $[S^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]$, which in the page's $3$-regular labels $(3),(2,1)$ is the matrix $$\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ ([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]); the group-side entries are verified directly from the two-dimensional model $S^{(2,1)}$ of characteristic $3$, whose all-ones vector spans a trivial submodule with sign quotient, together with $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$ and $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$.

No choice principle is used.

Complete current authored claim and local proof (not a citation-only sketch), guarded carrier research/frontier-44-special-representation-examples-28-owner-step3-cellular-branching-bindings-round1/coherent-round1/after/ex-a-weight-one-block-decomposition-matrix.md SHA256 c3d41cb4c11855186570911145c03bcac1d05f7c21ed27137634bcdb39c000c3. The original scaffold strategy is retained byte-exactly in the authentic preimage and protected history; this current authored-proof instantiation does not reset any prior review counter.

## Example

Take $e=p=3$ and the weight-one configuration $n=3$, $\gamma=\varnothing$ of [[thm-weight-one-block-decomposition-pattern]]; the three partitions of $3$ with $3$-core $\varnothing$ are $\lambda_1=(3)\rhd\lambda_2=(2,1)\rhd\lambda_3=(1,1,1)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). The associated q-Schur weight-one class at $p=3$ (with $d\ge3$) has the complete Weyl/simple decomposition matrix, with rows and columns in the order $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, equal to $$\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$ Applying the Schur functor and the conjugation/duality dictionary gives the Murphy Specht rows $[S^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]$, which in the page's $3$-regular labels $(3),(2,1)$ is the matrix $$\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ ([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]); the group-side entries are verified directly from the two-dimensional model $S^{(2,1)}$ of characteristic $3$, whose all-ones vector spans a trivial submodule with sign quotient, together with $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$ and $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$.

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The prime $p=e=3$, the partitions $(3)$, $(2,1)$, $(1,1,1)$ of $n=3$, and the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F$ of $S_F(d,3)$ for $d\ge3$ over any field $F$ of characteristic $3$, with $q=1$ and quantum characteristic $e=3$ (for example $F=\mathbb F_3$).

[F1] $3$-cores: the $3$-core of a partition is computed by removing rim $3$-hooks until none remains; $C_3((3))=\varnothing$, $C_3((2,1))=\varnothing$, $C_3((1,1,1))=\varnothing$, and these are all the partitions of $3$ with core $\varnothing$, ordered by dominance as $(3)\rhd(2,1)\rhd(1,1,1)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]).

[F2] The weight-one pattern [[thm-weight-one-block-decomposition-pattern]] applied with $e=3$, $\gamma=\varnothing$: in the source's normalisation $W^{(1,1,1)}=L^{(1,1,1)}$ and $[W^{(3)}]=[L^{(3)}]+[L^{(2,1)}]$, $[W^{(2,1)}]=[L^{(2,1)}]+[L^{(1,1,1)}]$.

[F3] Schur functor and dictionary ([[thm-weight-one-block-decomposition-pattern]]): the functor sends $W^{\lambda}_F$ to $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$, $L^{\lambda}_F$ to $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ or $0$, with $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}=0$ exactly for the non-$e$-restricted $\lambda$, and the Dipper-James module of this page is the signed $\theta$-pullback of the Murphy module of conjugate shape; for $e=3$ the non-$3$-restricted partition among $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ is $(3)$, while $(2,1)$ and $(1,1,1)$ are $3$-restricted.

[F4] Group side: the simple $k[S_3]$-modules at $p=3$ are $D^{(3)}$ and $D^{(2,1)}$, indexed by the $3$-regular partitions $(3),(2,1)$ ([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]).

[F5] Tabloid model: the permutation module $M^{(2,1)}_k$ over a field $k$ has the three tabloids $v_1,v_2,v_3$ as a basis, where $v_i$ is the tabloid whose singleton second row is $\{i\}$, and $\sigma\cdot v_i=v_{\sigma(i)}$; the Specht module $S^{(2,1)}_k\subseteq M^{(2,1)}_k$ has basis $e_t=v_3-v_1$ and $e_u=v_2-v_1$. Moreover $S^{(3)}_k$ is the trivial module and $S^{(1,1,1)}_k$ is the sign module ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]], [[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]).



## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The labels and their cores. The hook-length diagrams of the three partitions of $3$ are $3,2,1$ for $(3)$; $3,1$ in the first row and $1$ in the second for $(2,1)$; and $3,2,1$ vertically for $(1,1,1)$. In each case there is exactly one hook of length $3$ and removing its rim hook leaves the empty partition, so all three partitions have $3$-core $\varnothing$; conversely any partition of $3$ with core $\varnothing$ is one of these, since a partition whose core has size $3$ is its own core, and $\varnothing$ has size $0=3-3$. Dominance orders them as $(3)\rhd(2,1)\rhd(1,1,1)$. [given, F1]

2.1 The Weyl matrix. By [F2] the Weyl classes in the simple basis are $[W^{(1,1,1)}]=(0,0,1)$, $[W^{(2,1)}]=(0,1,1)$ and $[W^{(3)}]=(1,1,0)$ with rows and columns ordered $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$; hence the decomposition matrix of this weight-one class is the displayed matrix with rows $(1,1,0),(0,1,1),(0,0,1)$, whose diagonal entries are $1$ and whose only off-diagonal nonzero entries are at positions $(1,2)$ and $(2,3)$, each equal to $1$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Murphy rows. By [F3] and step 1.1 the functor kills exactly $L^{(3)}$ among the three simple labels, so applying it to the rows of step 2.1 gives $[S^{(3)}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{(2,1)}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{(2,1)}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{(2,1)}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{(1,1,1)}_{\mathrm M}]$ and $[S^{(1,1,1)}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{(1,1,1)}_{\mathrm M}]$. [F3, step 2.1]

4.1 Dipper-James rows and the direct group computation. Conjugating the partitions $(3)\leftrightarrow(1,1,1)$, $(2,1)\leftrightarrow(2,1)$ and applying the signed $\theta$-pullback to every Hecke module, the rows of step 3.1 become $[S^{(1,1,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]$, $[S^{(2,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]+[D^{(3)}]$ and $[S^{(3)}]=[D^{(3)}]$ in the $3$-regular labels, that is, the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ and columns $(3),(2,1)$. For the independent direct check, put $w:=e_t+e_u=v_3-v_1+v_2-v_1=v_1+v_2+v_3$ in characteristic $3$: then $w\ne0$ spans a one-dimensional submodule, since $\sigma\cdot v_i=v_{\sigma(i)}$ gives $\sigma\cdot w=w$ for every $\sigma\in S_3$, so it realises the trivial module; and in the quotient, $(12)\cdot e_t+e_t=(v_3-v_2)+(v_3-v_1)=2v_3-v_1-v_2=3v_3-w\equiv0$ shows that $(12)$ acts by $-1$, so the quotient is the sign module. With $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F5], and $D^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $D^{(2,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F4], the direct rows of $S^{(3)},S^{(2,1)},S^{(1,1,1)}$ are $(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$, matching the matrix obtained from the Schur functor entry by entry. [F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

before_object.title: Murphy cells are the same-shape contragredient Specht duals
before_object.statement: For every commutative $R$, unit $q$ and partition $\lambda$ there is an explicit perfect $R$-bilinear star-balanced pairing $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\times P(\lambda)\to R$, giving $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ naturally under all coefficient-ring base changes. Equivalently, the kernel of the row-permutation quotient onto $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is the orthogonal complement of $P(\lambda)$ for the independently defined permutation form, and its preimage in $M(\lambda)$ is $M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$. The pairing matrix on the actual standard bases has determinant a unit in $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$; its entries and inverse are given by finite tableau formulas. No nondegeneracy of the form restricted to $P(\lambda)$ is required. No choice principle is used.

# NEW50 ordinary DJ/Murphy bridge construction

Author: `/root/repair_cell_head_classification/native50_pairing_constructor`.
Scope: the two bridge theorem IDs assigned by the parent. This note writes no native prototype, gate, state, decision, source-attempt counter or source20 carrier. It is a construction, not an independent audit. The integral constructor's final carrier was read and its Sections 1 and 3 checked as described below. The independent Murphy cellular prerequisite remains a parent-owned prerequisite check.

Work over A=Z[q,q^{-1}]. Put μ=λ', L=ell(wλ), N=ell(w0(Sμ)), and Pν(q)=Σ_{u∈Sν}q^{ell(u)}. Use exactly the rowmodule, DJ generator, Murphy quotient, star and θ normalizations of NEW50. In particular z=xλ T_wλ yμ, θ(Ti)=q−1−Ti, and θ(xμ)=q^N yμ. All coefficient computations below are in this Laurent ring; no quantum factorial is inverted in the integral module construction.

## Exact integral input and its boundary

The independent integral constructor supplies these precise lemmas in `../integral-constructor/constructive-proof.md`, Sections 1 and 3:

* xα H yν=0 whenever α is not dominated by ν'. This is a Laurent-polynomial identity proved by minimal double cosets and a row/column collision, with the factor (1+Ti)(1−q^{-1}Ti)=0.
* For t standard of shape μ, e_t=z T_{d(t)} has rowtabloid support weakly below t' in tableau-prefix dominance, with coefficient q^{ell(d(t))} at t'. Thus the minor obtained by projecting onto the standard λ rowtabloids is triangular with diagonal Laurent units. The e_t are independent and their span is a split submodule of Mλ.

The signed cell surjection constructed next supplies the missing spanning assertion. Consequently these two input lemmas, together with the independent Murphy cellular basis, prove the full split free DJ basis; this avoids assuming a DJ spanning theorem before using the map that proves it. The formula indexes e_t by standard μ tableaux, not by rowreading d(t) for standard λ tableaux.

## Signed conjugate map, with no guessed relations

The sign-twisted cell module identifies with θ(Mμ)/θ(Kμ), where Kμ=Mμ∩I^{▷μ}, via a↦θ(a). On θ(Mμ) define

F(θ(xμ)h)=q^{-N} xλ T_wλ θ(xμ)h=z h.

This is well defined as literal left multiplication followed by multiplication by a Laurent unit. Every higher Murphy basis element of shape ν▷μ has the form T_a^* xν T_b; its θ-image is a Laurent unit times θ(T_a)^* yν θ(T_b). The annihilation lemma gives xλ H yν=0, because ν▷λ' implies λ is not dominated by ν'. Therefore xλ T_wλ θ(I^{▷μ})=0, so F kills θ(Kμ). It induces an H-linear surjection C_M(μ)^θ→Pλ with F(c0)=z. It is surjective because z generates Pλ.

Let E=span(e_t), and let π:Mλ→E be the explicit retraction obtained by inverting the unit triangular pivot matrix. The composite πF:C_M(μ)^θ→E is surjective, because F is onto Pλ and E⊂Pλ. Both modules are free of rank f^μ. Choose the finitely many preimages of the basis vectors of E: their coordinate columns form a right inverse of the square matrix of πF. Taking determinants shows that its determinant is a unit, hence πF is an isomorphism. If p∈Pλ and π(p)=0, choose u with F(u)=p; injectivity of πF gives u=0 and p=0. For any p∈Pλ the difference p−π(p) is in this kernel, so Pλ=E. This proves simultaneously that F is an isomorphism and Pλ is split free. No field rank calculation is used.

Define Φλ=F^{-1}. Then Φλ(z)=c0 and, for every h∈H,

Φλ(z h)=c0 θ(h),

where the right side is computed using the ordinary action on C_M(μ), and regarded as a vector in its θ twist. In particular Φλ(e_t)=c0 θ(T_{d(t)}). This is an actual relation-respecting map, not an assignment to the untransformed Murphy standard vector c_t. The latter assignment would generally be wrong.

For any R and unit q_R, tensor this isomorphism. Because Pλ is split in Mλ and Mλ is split free in H by the distinguished coset basis, its tensor image is exactly the actual right ideal z_R H_R. The Murphy quotient, its higher kernel and their bases commute with base change. Hence the result holds over every commutative coefficient ring, including rings with zero divisors.

## Same-shape perfect cross-pairing

Let τ:H→A take the coefficient of T_1. The standard-basis multiplication gives τ(T_u^* T_v)=δ_{u,v}q^{ell(u)}, and τ(ab)=τ(ba). These identities follow by induction from the quadratic multiplication rule. For distinguished d,e∈Dλ, length-additive row-coset multiplication gives

τ(T_d^* xλ T_e)=δ_{d,e}q^{ell(d)}.

Therefore, for a=xλ h and b=xλ g,

τ(a^*b)=Pλ(q) β(a,b).

This equality is first a polynomial identity on distinguished basis vectors and then follows by bilinearity.

If a∈Kλ=Mλ∩I^{▷λ} and p∈Pλ, then a^*p=0. Indeed every higher Murphy element of shape ν▷λ is T_r^* xν T_s, and each product with p=xλ T_wλ yλ' h vanishes by xν H yλ'=0, since ν is not dominated by λ. Thus Pλ(q) β(a,p)=0. The Laurent ring is a domain and Pλ(q) is a nonzero Laurent polynomial, so β(a,p)=0. No cancellation is performed in a specialized ring: the identity is established universally and then specialized with the supplied base-change-compatible kernel basis.

The formula

Bλ(a+Kλ,p)=β(a,p)

is consequently well defined and star-balanced. It gives a homomorphism C_M(λ)→Pλ^circ. The diagonal matrix of β on the rowmodule has unit entries q^{ell(d)}, so Mλ→Mλ^* is an isomorphism. Since Pλ is a split submodule, restriction Mλ^*→Pλ^* is surjective. Hence Mλ→Pλ^* is surjective, and because Kλ is killed it factors as a surjection C_M(λ)→Pλ^circ. Both are free of rank f^λ. Its determinant is a unit, hence it is an isomorphism. Its kernel in Mλ is exactly Kλ=Pλ^⊥. After every base change the same inverse matrix proves perfectness and the same kernel identity.

This is a genuine perfect cross-pairing and requires no nondegeneracy of the restricted DJ form. Explicit entries on the actual bases are finite formulas: expand e_t in the distinguished rowbasis as e_t=Σ_d a_{td} xλT_d; for a standard λ tableau s,

Bλ(c_s,e_t)=q^{ell(d(s))}a_{t,d(s)}.

The coefficients a_{td} are obtained by expanding the finite signed symmetrizer and the word T_wλ T_u T_{d(t)} with the quadratic multiplication rules. The inverse pairing matrix is det(B)^{-1}adj(B); det(B) is a Laurent unit by the preceding proof. This is a finite tableau formula, not an unspecified inverse in a generic field.

## Universal form identity and the exact unit

The initial DJ generator expands as

z=Σ_{u∈Sμ}(-q)^{-ell(u)} xλ T_{wλu}.

Each wλu is distinguished for the λ rowmodule, these cosets are distinct, and ell(wλu)=L+ell(u). To see rowstandardness, each λ row picks one entry from each consecutive interval corresponding to a column of λ; permuting within the separate intervals preserves its increasing order. Minimality and length additivity are the standard minimal-double-coset property. Thus

β(z,z)=q^L Σ_{u∈Sμ}q^{-ell(u)}=q^{L-N}Pμ(q).

The last equality pairs u with w0(Sμ)u. On the independent Murphy cell, xμ^2=Pμ(q)xμ gives Gμ(c0,c0)=Pμ(q). Therefore the only possible proportionality factor with Φ(z)=c0 is

uλ(q)=q^{N-L}.

Here is a choice-free local justification that the comparison of generator norms determines the whole form, without using generic rank to establish an integral lattice claim. Over K=Q(q), the regular trace bilinear form (a,b)↦Tr_K(L_ab) has determinant a polynomial nonzero at q=1: there H is Q[S_n], where its standard-basis matrix is n! times the permutation matrix pairing u with u^{-1}. Thus this form is nondegenerate over K. The Jacobson radical of a finite-dimensional algebra is nilpotent; for a in that radical and any b, L_ab is nilpotent and has trace zero. Nondegeneracy forces the radical to vanish, so H_K is semisimple.

In a semisimple cellular algebra every cell form is nondegenerate and the cell module has full matrix algebra acting on it. One can verify this directly, without a splitting-field or absolute-choice assumption: linearly extend the finite cell order and take the corresponding successive semisimple quotient ideals. A cell layer is C⊗C with multiplication (a⊗b)(c⊗d)=G(b,c)a⊗d. If G were degenerate, (rad G)⊗C would be a nonzero square-zero ideal stable under the surrounding algebra by contravariance and the cell law. This contradicts semisimplicity of the quotient. Invertibility of G then realizes every rank-one operator, so every module endomorphism of C is scalar. This also proves that any two nonzero contravariant forms on C are proportional: use one nonsingular Gram matrix to turn the other into a commuting endomorphism.

After the integral isomorphism F has been established, transfer β to C_M(μ)^θ. The Murphy form Gμ is nondegenerate generically, and the transferred form is nonzero because its initial value q^{L-N}Pμ(q) is nonzero. The preceding endomorphism calculation makes the forms proportional over K. Comparing their initial values gives, for all integral x,y∈Pλ,

Gμ^θ(Φλx,Φλy)=q^{N-L}β(x,y).

Both sides have entries in A. Their equality over its fraction field implies equality in A, so tensoring proves the identity over every commutative R with unit parameter. This method neither divides by Pμ after specialization nor discards a lattice index. It uses generic semisimplicity only for uniqueness of an already integral pair of forms.

## Consequences, including all fields at q=1

The form identity multiplies by a unit, so after every coefficient specialization Φ sends the DJ form radical exactly onto the radical of the twisted conjugate Murphy form. The quotient isomorphism includes the zero-quotient case. Over a PID, for a chosen prime π and every i≥0, x lies in the ith divisibility submodule precisely when β(x,P)⊂π^i; the unit-scaled identity and the isomorphism Φ make this equivalent to the corresponding Murphy condition. Thus all these submodules and reductions correspond.

The perfect pairing gives C_M(λ)≅Pλ^circ; the signed conjugate map for λ' gives Pλ'≅C_M(λ)^θ. Combining them yields Pλ'≅Pλ^{circ,θ}. The conjugate cell itself satisfies C_M(λ')≅Pλ^θ, without an additional dual.

At q=1, all exponents give unit 1, θ is the sign automorphism, and the permutation form is the usual tabloid form. Consequently the module and form comparisons hold over every field, including characteristic two and cases where the form radical is the whole module. Empty shapes use L=N=0 and the scalar 1.

## Current completion boundary

The final integral carrier was read. Its collision factorization in Section 1 and its prefix-count induction in Section 3 check correctly. For completeness, the standard ascending chain used there exists as follows: view standard tableaux as linear extensions of the Young-node partial order. Bubble-sort the desired extension toward rowreading order by adjacent inversions. Any swapped pair is incomparable, because comparable nodes have the same order in both linear extensions. Each swap removes one inversion relative to rowreading; reversing the sorting supplies an ascending standard chain from t^μ, with the exact additive-length permutations required in Section 3. In particular every transpose swap has i in the lower row and i+1 in the upper row, so the q coefficient and the two prefix-count bounds used in that proof apply.

after_object.title: Murphy cells are the same-shape contragredient Specht duals
after_object.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with its basis $\{m_t\}$, $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$, the permutation form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ and the DJ form on $P(\lambda)$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]. Then:

1. Setting $B_\lambda(m_s,p):=\beta(x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(s)},p)$ for $s\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ and $p\in P(\lambda)$ defines an explicit $R$-bilinear pairing $B_\lambda\colon C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\times P(\lambda)\to R$ that is $H$-balanced, $B_\lambda(mh,p)=B_\lambda(m,ph^*)$, and whose adjoint $c\mapsto B_\lambda(c,-)$ is an isomorphism of right $H$-modules $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ onto the star-contragredient module of [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. No nondegeneracy of the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ is required.

2. ## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, $q\in R^\times$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with its standard basis, star anti-involution, the modules $M(\lambda)=x_\lambda H\supseteq P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$, the distinguished basis $\{b_r=x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(r)}\}$ of $M(\lambda)$ and the permutation form $\beta$, the Murphy basis $\{m^\rho_{st}\}$, the dominance ideal $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with basis $\{m_s\}$ and the Murphy form $G_\lambda$.

[F1] The trace $\tau\colon H\to R$, $\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$, satisfies $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ and $\tau(a^*b)=B_0(a,b)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ for standard basis elements $a=T_u$, $b=T_v$; the bilinear form $\tau(a^*b)$ has unit diagonal in the standard basis ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F2] $M(\lambda)$ is free on $\{b_r\}$, $\beta(b_r,b_v)=\delta_{r,v}q^{\ell(d_\lambda(r))}$, and $\beta$ is $H$-contravariant; $P(\lambda)$ is free on $\{e_t=z_\lambda T_{d_\lambda'(t)}\}$ and a split direct summand of $M(\lambda)$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]], [[lem-dj-bridge-permutation-form-invariance-and-restriction]], [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]).
