[F5] The star-contragredient $N^\circ=\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,R)$ of a right $H$-module is a right $H$-module via $(fh)(m)=f(mh^*)$; for finite free $N$ it is finite free of the same rank and $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]).





## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The correctly scaled universal trace formula.** Work first over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$, using $q=v$ as the formal parameter. For $d,e\in D_\lambda$, length additivity gives $b_d=\sum_{u\in S_\lambda}T_{ud}$, and [F1] gives $\tau(b_d^*b_e)=0$ when $d\ne e$, while $\tau(b_d^*b_d)=\sum_{u\in S_\lambda}q^{\ell(ud)}=q^{\ell(d)}P_\lambda(q)$, where $P_\lambda(q):=\sum_{u\in S_\lambda}q^{\ell(u)}$. By bilinearity, $$\tau(a^*b)=P_\lambda(q)\,\beta(a,b)\qquad(a,b\in M_A(\lambda)).$$ The factor $P_\lambda$ is essential; it is not generally a unit and can vanish after specialization. It is nonzero in the domain $A$, since its constant coefficient is $1$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 **Orthogonality before specialization.** Put $K_A=M_A(\lambda)\cap I_A^{\rhd\lambda}$ and $p=z_\lambda h$. For a higher Murphy element $m^\nu_{uv}=T_{d_\nu(u)}^*x_\nu T_{d_\nu(v)}$ with $\nu\rhd\lambda$, its product with $p$ after star is $$ (m^\nu_{uv})^*p=T_{d_\nu(v)}^*x_\nu\bigl(T_{d_\nu(u)}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\bigr)y_{\lambda'}h=0,$$ because $x_\nu Hy_{\lambda'}=0$ by [F4]. The outer factor multiplies a zero vector; no factor is silently discarded. Expand $k\in K_A$ in the higher Murphy basis using [F3]. Then $k^*p=0$ and step 1.1 gives $P_\lambda(q)\beta(k,p)=0$. Cancel this nonzero polynomial only in the universal domain $A$, proving $\beta(K_A,P_A)=0$. The quotient and its kernel in [F3] are base-change compatible: the quotient is free on the supplied standard basis, its kernel is the split kernel of that quotient, and the independent Murphy construction identifies its specialization with $M_R(\lambda)\cap I_R^{\rhd\lambda}$. Thus tensoring the zero pairing identity gives $\beta(K_R,P_R)=0$ for every $R$ and unit $q$. No cancellation is performed in $R$, including when $P_\lambda(q)=0$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 **The descended pairing is perfect.** Define $B_\lambda(a+K_R,p)=\beta(a,p)$; step 2.1 proves this is well defined. Contravariance gives $B_\lambda(ch,p)=B_\lambda(c,ph^*)$, so its adjoint $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ is an $H$-homomorphism by [F5]. The map $M(\lambda)\to M(\lambda)^\circ$, $a\mapsto\beta(a,-)$, is an isomorphism with unit diagonal $q^{\ell(d)}$. Consequently these two input lemmas, together with the independent Murphy cellular basis, prove the full split free DJ basis; this avoids assuming a DJ spanning theorem before using the map that proves it. This is well defined as literal left multiplication followed by multiplication by a Laurent unit. Every higher Murphy basis element of shape ν▷μ has the form T_a^* xν T_b; its θ-image is a Laurent unit times θ(T_a)^* yν θ(T_b). Taking determinants shows that its determinant is a unit, hence πF is an isomorphism. If p∈Pλ and π(p)=0, choose u with F(u)=p; injectivity of πF gives u=0 and p=0. For any p∈Pλ the difference p−π(p) is in this kernel, so Pλ=E. This proves simultaneously that F is an isomorphism and Pλ is split free. No field rank calculation is used.

Define Φλ=F^{-1}. Then Φλ(z)=c0 and, for every h∈H,

Φλ(z h)=c0 θ(h),

where the right side is computed using the ordinary action on C_M(μ), and regarded as a vector in its θ twist. In particular Φλ(e_t)=c0 θ(T_{d(t)}). This is an actual relation-respecting map, not an assignment to the untransformed Murphy standard vector c_t. The latter assignment would generally be wrong.

Let τ:H→A take the coefficient of T_1. The standard-basis multiplication gives τ(T_u^* T_v)=δ_{u,v}q^{ell(u)}, and τ(ab)=τ(ba). These identities follow by induction from the quadratic multiplication rule. For distinguished d,e∈Dλ, length-additive row-coset multiplication gives

τ(T_d^* xλ T_e)=δ_{d,e}q^{ell(d)}.

τ(a^*b)=Pλ(q) β(a,b).

This equality is first a polynomial identity on distinguished basis vectors and then follows by bilinearity.

If a∈Kλ=Mλ∩I^{▷λ} and p∈Pλ, then a^*p=0. Indeed every higher Murphy element of shape ν▷λ is T_r^* xν T_s, and each product with p=xλ T_wλ yλ' h vanishes by xν H yλ'=0, since ν is not dominated by λ. No cancellation is performed in a specialized ring: the identity is established universally and then specialized with the supplied base-change-compatible kernel basis.

The formula

Bλ(a+Kλ,p)=β(a,p)

is consequently well defined and star-balanced. It gives a homomorphism C_M(λ)→Pλ^circ. The diagonal matrix of β on the rowmodule has unit entries q^{ell(d)}, so Mλ→Mλ^* is an isomorphism. Since Pλ is a split submodule, restriction Mλ^*→Pλ^* is surjective. Hence Mλ→Pλ^* is surjective, and because Kλ is killed it factors as a surjection C_M(λ)→Pλ^circ. Both are free of rank f^λ. Its determinant is a unit, hence it is an isomorphism. Its kernel in Mλ is exactly Kλ=Pλ^⊥. After every base change the same inverse matrix proves perfectness and the same kernel identity.

This is a genuine perfect cross-pairing and requires no nondegeneracy of the restricted DJ form. Explicit entries on the actual bases are finite formulas: expand e_t in the distinguished rowbasis as e_t=Σ_d a_{td} xλT_d; for a standard λ tableau s,

The coefficients a_{td} are obtained by expanding the finite signed symmetrizer and the word T_wλ T_u T_{d(t)} with the quadratic multiplication rules. The inverse pairing matrix is det(B)^{-1}adj(B); det(B) is a Laurent unit by the preceding proof. This is a finite tableau formula, not an unspecified inverse in a generic field.

## Universal form identity and the exact unit

The initial DJ generator expands as

z=Σ_{u∈Sμ}(-q)^{-ell(u)} xλ T_{wλu}.

Each wλu is distinguished for the λ rowmodule, these cosets are distinct, and ell(wλu)=L+ell(u). To see rowstandardness, each λ row picks one entry from each consecutive interval corresponding to a column of λ; permuting within the separate intervals preserves its increasing order. Minimality and length additivity are the standard minimal-double-coset property. Thus

β(z,z)=q^L Σ_{u∈Sμ}q^{-ell(u)}=q^{L-N}Pμ(q).

The last equality pairs u with w0(Sμ)u. On the independent Murphy cell, xμ^2=Pμ(q)xμ gives Gμ(c0,c0)=Pμ(q). Therefore the only possible proportionality factor with Φ(z)=c0 is

uλ(q)=q^{N-L}.

Here is a choice-free local justification that the comparison of generator norms determines the whole form, without using generic rank to establish an integral lattice claim. Thus this form is nondegenerate over K. The Jacobson radical of a finite-dimensional algebra is nilpotent; for a in that radical and any b, L_ab is nilpotent and has trace zero. Nondegeneracy forces the radical to vanish, so H_K is semisimple.

In a semisimple cellular algebra every cell form is nondegenerate and the cell module has full matrix algebra acting on it. One can verify this directly, without a splitting-field or absolute-choice assumption: linearly extend the finite cell order and take the corresponding successive semisimple quotient ideals. A cell layer is C⊗C with multiplication (a⊗b)(c⊗d)=G(b,c)a⊗d. Invertibility of G then realizes every rank-one operator, so every module endomorphism of C is scalar. This also proves that any two nonzero contravariant forms on C are proportional: use one nonsingular Gram matrix to turn the other into a commuting endomorphism.

After the integral isomorphism F has been established, transfer β to C_M(μ)^θ. The preceding endomorphism calculation makes the forms proportional over K. Comparing their initial values gives, for all integral x,y∈Pλ,

Gμ^θ(Φλx,Φλy)=q^{N-L}β(x,y).

Both sides have entries in A. Their equality over its fraction field implies equality in A, so tensoring proves the identity over every commutative R with unit parameter. This method neither divides by Pμ after specialization nor discards a lattice index. It uses generic semisimplicity only for uniqueness of an already integral pair of forms.

The form identity multiplies by a unit, so after every coefficient specialization Φ sends the DJ form radical exactly onto the radical of the twisted conjugate Murphy form. The quotient isomorphism includes the zero-quotient case. At q=1, all exponents give unit 1, θ is the sign automorphism, and the permutation form is the usual tabloid form. Consequently the module and form comparisons hold over every field, including characteristic two and cases where the form radical is the whole module. Empty shapes use L=N=0 and the scalar 1.

## Statement

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. 2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. **Given:** A commutative ring $R$, $q\in R^\times$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with conjugate $\mu=\lambda'$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, the modules $M(\lambda)\supseteq P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with the distinguished and polytabloid bases, the permutation form $\beta$ and its restriction $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with basis $\{m_t\}$ and Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$.

Its $H$-linearity with the twisted target action gives $\Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)$, where this expression uses the ordinary action on the underlying Murphy module. At $v=1$ its matrix is $n!$ times the permutation matrix $u\leftrightarrow u^{-1}$: in the regular group basis left multiplication by a nonidentity group element has trace zero, whereas the identity has trace $n!$. Its determinant is therefore nonzero, so the regular trace form is nonsingular over $K$. If $a\in J(H_K)$, every $ab$ is nilpotent by [F6], and $L_{ab}$ has trace zero; nondegeneracy forces $a=0$, so $H_K$ is semisimple. ## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$ or a commutative ring $R$ with a unit $q$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, the module $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its basis $\{e_t\}$, its DJ form and its form quotient $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with basis $\{m_t\}$ and form quotient $D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$, the sign automorphism $\theta$, and the isomorphism and unit identity of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]].

[F1] $\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ is an $H$-module isomorphism with $G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)$ and $u_\lambda(q)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F2] $\theta$ is the involutive sign automorphism; the twist $M^\theta$ has action $m\cdot h=m\theta(h)$, is exact, preserves composition multiplicities and maps simple modules to simple modules; at $q=1$ over a field, $\theta$ is the pullback along $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]).

[F3] $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ has the standard polytabloids as a $\mathbb Z$-basis and is base-change compatible: for every commutative ring $R$ the canonical map $R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\to R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ is injective onto the span of the polytabloids in the tabloid module, and the standard polytabloids form an $R$-basis of the image ([[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]]).

[F4] The conjugate-sign dictionary $S^\lambda_F\otimes\operatorname{sgn}\cong(S^{\lambda'}_F)^*$ holds over every field, with the explicit sign-twisted tabloid homomorphism ([[lem-conjugate-specht-sign-duality-over-fields]]).

[F5] The Hecke algebra has presentation $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant commutation, with standard basis $(T_w)_w$; $S_n$ has the Coxeter presentation $s_i^2=1$ with the same braid and distant commutation relations ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-the-symmetric-group-has-the-coxeter-presentation]]). The row-module and polytabloid bases are split and compatible with every coefficient-ring base change ([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]], [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]).

The Coxeter presentation in [F5] therefore gives the homomorphism $H_{R,1}(S_n)\to R[S_n]$ carrying $T_i$ to $s_i$. A reduced word shows that it carries every $T_w$ to $w$. These are bases of the source and target over $R$, so the map is an isomorphism over $R$, including in positive characteristic and with zero divisors. Equivalently the assignment $s_i\mapsto T_i$ gives its inverse directly from the presentation. No complex-field specialization, dimension comparison over a field or semisimplicity is used. [F5, algebra]

1.2 **Multiplicities and zero quotients.** For a field and unit $q$, the unit form identity in [F1] identifies $D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ with $(D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including zero quotients. A nonzero cell-form quotient is simple: the cell rank-one action shows that every vector outside its radical generates the cell module, so the radical is its unique maximal submodule. Thus when $D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$, the module $D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ is a legitimate simple composition-factor label. Applying the exact twist equivalence in [F2] to a composition series and using [F1] gives $$[P(\lambda):D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta:D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):(D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}].$$ This proves clause 2. 2.1 **The actual polytabloids and the forms.** Give the classical tabloid module the right action $\{t\}\cdot w=\{w^{-1}\cdot t\}=\{t\cdot w\}$. It respects the right action: at $q=1$ the row-module multiplication rule is simply the permutation of these cosets, with a same-row transposition acting as $1$. Every diagonal value of $\beta$ becomes $1$, so this is an isometry to the orthonormal tabloid form. The column group of the column-filled tableau $t_\lambda$ is exactly $S_{\lambda'}$, because its columns carry the consecutive row blocks of $\lambda'$. Hence $z_\lambda=x_\lambda w_\lambda\sum_{u\in S_{\lambda'}}\operatorname{sgn}(u)u$ maps to $\sum_u\operatorname{sgn}(u)\{t_\lambda\cdot u\}$, the classical column polytabloid of $t_\lambda$ (replace $u$ by $u^{-1}$ to compare with the left-action formula). Covariance shows $e_t=z_\lambda d_{\lambda'}(t)$ maps to the polytabloid of $t_\lambda\cdot d_{\lambda'}(t)=t'$, the transpose of the standard $\lambda'$-tableau $t$. 4.1 **Conditional Schur dictionary and conclusion.** Under the stated separate hypothesis on a Schur corner, its images at $\lambda'$ are $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and $D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$. before_object.title: Untwisted conjugation changes the module
before_object.statement: Over $\mathbb Q$ at $q=1$ and $n=3$, the Murphy cell module $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ is sign with $T_i=-1$, while the ordinary polytabloid module $P((3))$ and its contragredient dual are trivial with $T_i=1$. The correct bridge is $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$; combining it with same-shape duality gives $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$, which is a different formula. This reproduces the source20 countermodel from the standalone new foundations. No choice principle is used.
before_object.strategy: The top row symmetrizer $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}w$ spans $P((3))$ and is fixed by every permutation, so this module and its dual are trivial. In the one-dimensional bottom Murphy cell, the higher elements $1+s_1$ and $1+s_2$ vanish, so each $s_i=-1$. A module isomorphism from the bottom cell to the trivial module would intertwine these scalar operators; over $\mathbb Q$, $-1\ne1$, so no such nonzero isomorphism exists. The automorphism $\theta$ sends $s_i$ to $-s_i$ and therefore corrects the action. The general corrected formulas follow by the two separately proved bridge theorems, not by treating the ordinary Specht module as always self-dual. This finite counterexample uses no Schur theory or old convention definition.

## Statement refuted

**Refuted claim:** the same-shape duality $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ of [[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]] may be applied without a sign twist, i.e. one may conclude $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ directly.

This is false. Over $\mathbb Q$ at $q=1$ and $n=3$ the Murphy cell module $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ is the sign module, in which $T_i$ acts by $-1$, while the ordinary polytabloid module $P((3))$ and its contragredient dual are trivial, in which $T_i$ acts by $+1$. Hence $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ without $\theta$ fails in general. The correct bridge is $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$ of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]; combining it with same-shape duality gives $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$, which is a different formula. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field $\mathbb Q$, the specialization $q=1$ of the type-$A$ Hecke algebra $H$, the polytabloid module $P((3))=z_{(3)}H$ with its DJ form, the Murphy cell module $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ with its form, and the comparison theorem [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]] together with its corollary [[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]].

[F1] At $q=1$ the specialization of $H$ is the group algebra $\mathbb Q[S_3]$ and the sign automorphism $\theta$ is the pullback along $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$; the partitions $(3)$ and $(1^3)$ are conjugate ([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).

[F2] The comparison theorem gives $P((3))\cong C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ with the exact unit $u_{(3)}=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{(1^3)}))-\ell(w_{(3)})}$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F3] $P((3))=x_{(3)}H$ is spanned by $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$, and $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}$ for $i=1,2$; the contragredient dual of a one-dimensional module with trivial action is trivial ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F4] In $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ one has $f^{(1^3)}=1$, the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$ contains the elements $1+T_i$, and the cell form has value $G_{(1^3)}(m_0,m_0)=1$ ([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).



## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The ordinary module is trivial.** At $q=1$ one has $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$ and $x_{(3)}T_i=\sum_wT_wT_i=\sum_wT_{ws_i}=x_{(3)}$ for each generator, because right multiplication by $s_i$ permutes the group and every $T_{ws_i}$ is again one of the summed basis elements; with the scalar carried along this reads $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}=x_{(3)}$ at $q=1$, and $P((3))=x_{(3)}H=\mathbb Q\,x_{(3)}$ is one-dimensional. Its dual is therefore also one-dimensional with trivial action. [F3, algebra]

1.2 **The cell is sign.** At $q=1$ the element $1+T_i$ lies in the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$, because $1+T_1=x_{(2,1)}$ belongs to that two-sided ideal and conjugation by the invertible braid word $T_1T_2$ sends $T_1$ to $T_2$, so $1+T_2$ also belongs to it; hence in the one-dimensional cell $m_0(1+T_i)=0$, that is, $m_0T_i=-m_0$. The cell form value is $1$, and the module is the sign module. [F4, algebra]

2.1 **No untwisted isomorphism.** A right $H$-module isomorphism $f\colon C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))\to P((3))^\circ$ would satisfy $f(mh)=f(m)h$ for every $h$; taking $h=T_i$ and a nonzero $m$ gives $f(-m)=f(m)$ because $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ has $T_i$ acting by $-1$ and $P((3))^\circ$ has $T_i$ acting by $+1$, while $f(-m)=-f(m)$ in characteristic zero, so $-f(m)=f(m)$ forces $f(m)=0$, contradicting injectivity over $\mathbb Q$. Therefore no such isomorphism exists and the untwisted claim is false. The twisted statement is consistent: on $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ the generator $T_i$ acts by the ordinary action of $\theta(T_i)=-T_i$, that is by $+1$, matching $P((3))$, and the unit is $u_{(3)}=1$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

On $P((3))$ and $C_{\mathrm M}((3))$, both generators act by $q$; on $P((1^3))$ and $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$, both act by $-1$. ## Example

Let $H=H_{A,q}(S_3)$, $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$, and put $p_3(q)=(1+q)(1+q+q^2)$. All four modules $P((3)),P((1^3)),C_{\mathrm M}((3)),C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ have rank $1$. On $P((3))$ and $C_{\mathrm M}((3))$ both generators act by $q$; on $P((1^3))$ and $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ both act by $-1$. In the canonical generators $x_{(3)}$, $y_{(3)}$, $c_{(3)}$, $c_{(1^3)}$ the respective self-form values are $1$, $q^{-3}p_3(q)$, $p_3(q)$, $1$. Thus $\Phi_{(3)}(x_{(3)})=c_{(1^3)}$ has exact form multiplier $u_{(3)}=1$, whereas $\Phi_{(1^3)}(y_{(3)})=c_{(3)}$ has $u_{(1^3)}=q^3$. In both targets the action is twisted by $\theta$, so the two module identities match. At $q=1$ over $\mathbb Q$ the respective form values are $1,6,6,1$, and $\theta$ exchanges trivial and sign. These identities specialize over every commutative ring with a unit parameter. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The type-$A$ Hecke algebra $H$ of $S_3$ over $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ with generators $T_1,T_2$, the shapes $(3)$ and $(1^3)=(3)'$, their row and polytabloid modules and Murphy cells, the sign automorphism $\theta$ with $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i$, and the comparison theorem and its corollary [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]].

[F1] $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$ spans $P((3))=x_{(3)}H$ and $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}$ for $i=1,2$; the distinguished basis of $M((3))$ is $\{x_{(3)}\}$ with $\beta(x_{(3)},x_{(3)})=1$; the Murphy cell $C_{\mathrm M}((3))$ has one basis class $c_{(3)}=x_{(3)}+I^{\rhd(3)}$ and $G_{(3)}(c_{(3)},c_{(3)})=P_{(3)}(q)=p_3(q)$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F2] $x_{(1^3)}=1$, $y_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w$ spans $P((1^3))=y_{(3)}H$ and $y_{(3)}T_i=-y_{(3)}$ for $i=1,2$; the distinguished basis of $M((1^3))$ is the standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and $\beta(y_{(3)},y_{(3)})=q^{-3}p_3(q)$; the Murphy cell $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ has one basis class $c_{(1^3)}=1+I^{\rhd(1^3)}$ with $G_{(1^3)}(c_{(1^3)},c_{(1^3)})=1$ and $T_i$ acting by $-1$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).

[F3] The comparison theorem gives base-change compatible isomorphisms $\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ with $G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)$ and $u_\lambda(q)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}$, where the twisted action is $m\cdot h=m\theta(h)$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F4] For a right $H$-module $M$ and a unit $u$, a form identity $G(Mx,My)=u\beta(x,y)$ implies that the module actions of $H$ are intertwined along the same isomorphism; at $q=1$ over $\mathbb Q$ the specialization is the group algebra $\mathbb Q[S_3]$ and $\theta$ is the sign automorphism ([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).



## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Shape (3).** For the one-row shape, $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$ and right multiplication by $T_i$ permutes the sum, with the scalar rule $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}$ because every $T_wT_i$ recombines into $q$ times the full sum; since $z_{(3)}=x_{(3)}T_{w_{(3)}}y_{(1^3)}=x_{(3)}$ (here $w_{(3)}=1$ and $y_{(1^3)}=1$) the module $P((3))$ is the free rank-one module on $x_{(3)}$ with action $q$. Squaring gives $x_{(3)}^2=\sum_{v,w}T_vT_w=\sum_vT_vx_{(3)}=\bigl(\sum_vq^{\ell(v)}\bigr)x_{(3)}=p_3(q)x_{(3)}$, because the length distribution in $S_3$ is $(1,2,2,1)$ and $1+2q+2q^2+q^3=(1+q)(1+q+q^2)$; hence the Murphy cell has form value $G_{(3)}(c_{(3)},c_{(3)})=p_3(q)$ and action $q$, and $\beta(x_{(3)},x_{(3)})=1$ by [F1]. [F1, algebra]

1.2 **Shape (1^3).** For the one-column shape, $x_{(1^3)}=1$ and $P((1^3))=y_{(3)}H$ with $y_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w$. The pair argument $y_{(3)}T_i=\sum_{u}(-q)^{-\ell(u)}T_{us_i}$ over the two cosets of $\langle s_i\rangle$ gives $y_{(3)}T_i=-y_{(3)}$ for $i=1,2$, the sign representation of the rank-one module. The distinguished basis of $M((1^3))$ is the standard basis and $\beta$ is diagonal with entries $q^{\ell(w)}$, so $\beta(y_{(3)},y_{(3)})=\sum_wq^{-2\ell(w)}q^{\ell(w)}=\sum_wq^{-\ell(w)}=q^{-3}p_3(q)$, the last equality by $w\mapsto w_0w$. Modulo the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$, which contains $1+T_i$ because $1+T_1=x_{(2,1)}$ is a higher Murphy element and conjugation by the invertible braid word $T_1T_2$ sends $T_1$ to $T_2$, placing $1+T_2$ in the same two-sided ideal, the class $c_{(1^3)}$ satisfies $T_i=-1$ and $G_{(1^3)}(c_{(1^3)},c_{(1^3)})=P_{(1^3)}(q)=1$ by [F2]. [F2, algebra]

2.1 **The comparison maps.** By [F3] applied to $\lambda=(3)$, where $\lambda'=(1^3)$ and $\ell(w_0(S_{(1^3)}))=\ell(w_{(3)})=0$, the isomorphism $\Phi_{(3)}$ has unit $u_{(3)}=1$ and the identity $G^\theta_{(1^3)}(\Phi_{(3)}x_{(3)},\Phi_{(3)}x_{(3)})=\beta(x_{(3)},x_{(3)})=1$ is consistent because both sides are the value of the respective rank-one forms; explicitly $\Phi_{(3)}(x_{(3)})=c_{(1^3)}$ by [F3]. Applying it to $\lambda=(1^3)$, where $\lambda'=(3)$ and $\ell(w_0(S_{(3)}))=3$, $\ell(w_{(1^3)})=0$, gives $u_{(1^3)}=q^3$, and the identity $G_{(3)}(c_{(3)},c_{(3)})=q^3\,q^{-3}p_3(q)=p_3(q)$ is consistent; explicitly $\Phi_{(1^3)}(y_{(3)})=c_{(3)}$. In the target $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ the generator acts by the ordinary action of $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i=-T_i$, hence by $+1=q$ at $q=1$; in the target $C_{\mathrm M}((3))^\theta$ it acts by the ordinary action of $(q-1)-T_i$ on the class acting by $q$, hence by $(q-1)-q=-1$; these match the source actions $q$ on $P((3))$ and $-1$ on $P((1^3))$ computed in steps 1.1 and 1.2. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F3, algebra]

3.1 **Specialization and conclusion.** At $q=1$ over $\mathbb Q$ the four form values become $1$, $1^{-3}p_3(1)=6$, $6$ and $1$, and $\theta$ is the sign automorphism exchanging the trivial and sign modules, in agreement with [F4]; the module actions match as in step 2.1. Every displayed identity is an identity in $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ between Laurent polynomials, so all of them specialize along any ring map $A\to R$ with $q\mapsto q\in R^\times$. Only the rank-one computations, the trace-free form evaluations and the comparison theorem were used; no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, F1, F2, F3, F4] ∎

before_object.title: The two-tableau pairing at a singular parameter
before_object.statement:
For $\lambda=(2,1)$ put $x=1+T_1$ and $b_0=x$, $b_1=xT_2$, $b_2=xT_2T_1$ in the row permutation module. Its form is $\operatorname{diag}(1,q,q^2)$ and its generator action matrices, with coordinate row vectors, are $R_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&q&q-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $R_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1&0\\q&q-1&0\\0&0&q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The ordinary polytabloid basis is $p_0=z=xT_2(1-q^{-1}T_1)=b_1-q^{-1}b_2$, $p_1=zT_2=qb_0+(q-1)b_1-b_2$. Their embedding has unit determinant on its $b_0,b_2$ coordinates, and their form is
$$B=\begin{pmatrix}q+1&q^2\\q^2&q^3+q\end{pmatrix}.$$
In the Murphy quotient let $c_0=x$, $c_1=xT_2$ modulo the higher shape $(3)$. Its form and generator action matrices, with coordinate row vectors, are
$$G=\begin{pmatrix}q+1&-1\\-1&q^2+1\end{pmatrix},\quad M_1=\begin{pmatrix}q&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad M_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\q&q-1\end{pmatrix}.$$
On the ordinary basis the matrices are $P_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&0\\-q^2&q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $P_2=M_2$. The map $\Phi(p_0)=c_0$, $\Phi(p_1)=(q-1)c_0-c_1$ has matrix $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\q-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; it satisfies $P_iA=A((q-1)I-M_i)$ and $AGA^{\mathsf T}=B$. The same-shape perfect cross-pairing on the bases $(c_0,c_1)$ and $(p_0,p_1)$ has matrix $Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&q\\q&q(q-1)\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $-q^2$, a unit; its entries are the row-form coefficients before quotienting. Thus the exact self-form multiplier is1. Both Gram determinants equal $q(1+q+q^2)$. At $q=-1$ over characteristic zero these forms are nonsingular with determinant $-1$, even though $[2]_q=0$; at $q=1$ in characteristic2 both reduce to $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and have radical0. This distinguishes a singular algebra parameter from degeneracy of this particular module form. No choice principle is used.
before_object.strategy: The row module action follows by the Hecke quadratic and braid relations: $b_0T_1=qb_0$, $b_1T_1=b_2$, $b_2T_1=qb_1+(q-1)b_2$; $b_0T_2=b_1$, $b_1T_2=qb_0+(q-1)b_1$, $b_2T_2=qb_2$. Substituting the displayed $p_0,p_1$ gives $p_0T_1=-p_0$, $p_1T_1=-q^2p_0+qp_1$, $p_0T_2=p_1$, $p_1T_2=qp_0+(q-1)p_1$. The projection of $p_0,p_1$ onto coordinates $b_0,b_2$ has matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-q^{-1}\\q&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant1, proving a split free rank2 submodule over every ring. It contains the generator and is stable under both Hecke generators, so it is exactly $zH$, without using a general polytabloid-basis theorem. In the Murphy cell quotient the higher vector $x_{(3)}=b_0+b_1+b_2$ vanishes, so $b_2=-c_0-c_1$; the preceding action gives $M_i$. Cell multiplication gives $G_{00}=q+1$, $G_{01}=-1$, $G_{11}=q(q+1)-(q-1)=q^2+1$. Computing the row-basis weighted inner products gives $B$. Direct matrix multiplication verifies both intertwining identities and $AGA^{\mathsf T}=B$; $\det A=-1$ is a unit. Evaluating the two Gram matrices gives the stated radicals. Exact integer-polynomial verification is recorded separately in rank-three-symbolic-check.json; that finite check supports these calculations and is not a proof of the general comparison theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Hecke algebra $H=H_{R,q}(S_3)$ over a commutative ring $R$ with $q\in R^\times$, the shape $\lambda=(2,1)=\lambda'$, the row module $M(\lambda)$ with $x=x_\lambda=1+T_1$ and the distinguished basis $\{b_0,b_1,b_2\}$, the polytabloid module $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with $z_\lambda=xT_2(1-q^{-1}T_1)$, the permutation form $\beta$ and the Murphy cell $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with classes $c_0,c_1$ and form $G$, together with the comparison theorem and the perfect cross-pairing of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]] and [[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]].

[F1] $H$ has generators $T_1,T_2$ with $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid relation $T_1T_2T_1=T_2T_1T_2$ and standard basis $\{T_w\}$; $xT_1=q\,x$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]).

[F2] The distinguished basis $\{b_0,b_1,b_2\}=\{x,xT_{s_2},xT_{s_2s_1}\}$ of $M(\lambda)$ satisfies $\beta(b_i,b_j)=\delta_{ij}q^{i}$ and is the row basis of $D_\lambda=\{1,s_2,s_2s_1\}$ ([[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]).

[F3] $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ has basis $c_t=xT_{d(t)}$ for the standard tableaux $t$, and its form satisfies $m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G(c_s,c_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; the ideal $I^{\rhd\lambda}$ contains $x_{(3)}=b_0+b_1+b_2$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F4] $\Phi\colon P(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ is an isomorphism with $\Phi(z)=c_0$ and unit $u_\lambda(q)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}=q^{1-1}=1$ for $\lambda=(2,1)$; the pairing $B_\lambda(m_s,p)=\beta(xT_{d(s)},p)$ is perfect with the explicit entries $B_\lambda(c_s,e_t)=q^{\ell(d(s))}a_{d(s),t}$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]]).



## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Row module.** From [F1], $b_0T_1=xT_1=qx=q\,b_0$, $b_1T_1=xT_2T_1=b_2$ and $b_2T_1=xT_2T_1^2=xT_2((q-1)T_1+q)=(q-1)b_2+q\,b_1$; also $b_0T_2=b_1$, $b_1T_2=xT_2^2=x((q-1)T_2+q)=(q-1)b_1+q\,b_0$ and $b_2T_2=xT_2T_1T_2=xT_1T_2T_1=q\,xT_2T_1=q\,b_2$, using the braid relation. In the basis $(b_0,b_1,b_2)$ with coordinate row vectors these are exactly the matrices $R_1$ and $R_2$ of the statement, and $\beta(b_i,b_i)=q^{i}$ by [F2] because $\ell(1)=0$, $\ell(s_2)=1$, $\ell(s_2s_1)=2$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 **Polytabloids and their form.** Since $z_\lambda=xT_2(1-q^{-1}T_1)$ by [F4] and $y_{\lambda'}=1-q^{-1}T_1$, the displayed expressions $p_0=b_1-q^{-1}b_2$ and $p_1=zT_2=b_1T_2-q^{-1}b_2T_2=qb_0+(q-1)b_1-b_2$ follow from step 1.1. Their coordinates on $(b_0,b_2)$ give the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-q^{-1}\\q&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $q\cdot q^{-1}=1$, a unit over every $R$; hence the two polytabloids span a free rank-two split submodule stable under both generators, which by the comparison theorem is exactly $P(\lambda)=zH$. Weighted inner products against the diagonal form of [F2] give $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q+1&q^2\\q^2&q^3+q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$: explicitly $B_{00}=q+q^{-2}\cdot q^2=q+1$, $B_{01}=(q-1)q+q^2$ ... computing $(b_1-q^{-1}b_2,qb_0+(q-1)b_1-b_2)$ term by term gives $q(q-1)+q=q^2$, and $B_{11}=q^2+(q-1)^2q+q^2=q^3+q$. Its determinant is $q(q^2+q+1)$. [step 1.1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.2 **The Murphy quotient.** In $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ the higher vector $x_{(3)}=b_0+b_1+b_2$ vanishes by [F3], so $b_2=-c_0-c_1$ and $c_1=xT_2=b_1$. Then $c_0T_1=qx=q\,c_0$ and $c_1T_1=b_2=-c_0-c_1$, giving $M_1$; also $c_0T_2=c_1$ and $c_1T_2=(q-1)b_1+qb_0=(q-1)c_1+qc_0$, giving $M_2$. Expanding the defining products of [F3] in the Murphy basis and reading the coefficient of $m_{t_0t_0}=x$ gives $G(c_0,c_0)=q+1$ from $x^2=(q+1)x$, $G(c_0,c_1)=-1$ and $G(c_1,c_1)=q^2+1$; equivalently $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q+1&-1\\-1&q^2+1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $q^3+q^2+q$. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

3.1 **Comparison, cross-pairing and specializations.** The comparison theorem of [F4] gives $\Phi(z)=c_0$, hence $\Phi(p_1)=\Phi(zT_2)=c_0\theta(T_2)=(q-1)c_0-c_1$ and $A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\q-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$; direct matrix multiplication verifies $P_iA=A((q-1)I-M_i)$ for $i=1,2$ and $AGA^{\mathsf T}=B$, the latter being the form identity with the unit $u_\lambda=1$. The cross-pairing entries $B_\lambda(c_s,p_t)=\beta(b_{d(s)},p_t)$ on the standard bases give $Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&q\\q&q(q-1)\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $\det Q=-q^2\in A^\times$, so the pairing is perfect as in [F4]. The two Gram determinants agree with $q(1+q+q^2)$. At $q=-1$ in characteristic zero, $B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&-2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ have determinant $-1$, although $[2]_q=1+q=0$; at $q=1$ in characteristic $2$, both reduce to $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with determinant $1$, hence with zero radical. All identities are Laurent-polynomial identities, so they specialize to every $R$; no choice principle is used. [step 2.1, step 2.2, F4, algebra] ∎
